S.title: Efficacy of Medical Treatment Options for Reducing the Risk of Bleeding in Patients With Sporadic and Familial Cerebral Cavernous Malformations: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
S.abstract: Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) carry a significant hemorrhage risk. While surgery remains the primary treatment, deep-seated or eloquent lesions pose high operative risks, prompting interest in potential pharmacological approaches aimed at lesion stabilization. However, standardized medical management guidelines remain absent. This study evaluates the associations of statins, antithrombotics (ATs), and beta-blockers (BBs) with CCM hemorrhage risk. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO): CRD420251069357), a systematic review of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, and Scopus (inception to February 3, 2026) was conducted. Eligible studies compared bleeding outcomes in CCM patients receiving statins, ATs, or BBs versus no medical treatment. A multivariate meta-analysis utilized odds ratios (ORs) and surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) scores to evaluate follow-up (re)bleeding (primary outcome) and hemorrhagic presentation at diagnosis (secondary outcome). Seven studies (n = 3,092) were included. Statin therapy was associated with lower odds of follow-up (re)bleeding versus BBs (OR = 0.32, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.11-0.95) and no treatment (OR = 0.32, 95% CI: 0.14-0.73). Triple combination therapy (statin + AT + BB) was also associated with lower odds of (re)bleeding compared with no treatment (OR = 0.24, 95% CI: 0.06-0.95) and ranked highest according to SUCRA. Statin + AT was associated with lower (re)bleeding odds versus BBs (OR = 0.25, 95% CI: 0.09-0.73). Conversely, BB monotherapy was associated with higher odds of (re)bleeding compared with AT monotherapy (OR = 2.41, 95% CI: 1.13-5.10). Untreated patients had higher odds of hemorrhagic presentation compared with statin + AT (OR = 3.10, 95% CI: 1.31-7.39) and AT monotherapy (OR = 1.86, 95% CI: 1.09-3.13). In the SUCRA ranking, statin + AT had the lowest ranked risk of hemorrhagic presentation at diagnosis. In the absence of established pharmacological strategies, statin- and AT-based regimens were associated with lower CCM hemorrhage odds. However, the available evidence is predominantly observational and limited, with substantial potential for confounding by indication. Together with the null findings of the randomized AT CASH EPOC trial, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and are insufficient to guide clinical practice pending prospective randomized validation.

S.title: Quantitative Susceptibility Mapping of the Centromedian Nucleus and Indirect Comparison with Alternate Sequences.
S.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Neuromodulation of the thalamic centromedian nucleus (CM) is an established therapy for epilepsy and been applied for pain, Tourette syndrome, and disorders of consciousness. Accurate targeting remains challenging because CM is poorly visualized on conventional MRI sequences, necessitating reliance on indirect targeting approaches. Although advanced MRI sequences, such as magnetization-prepared rapid acquisition of two gradient echoes (MP2RAGE) and white matter null (WMn), have been explored, they fail to reliably delineate the boundary between CM and lateral thalamus, a region associated with optimal stimulation outcomes, particularly in epilepsy. Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) has emerged as a promising technique for differentiating thalamic nuclei based on tissue magnetic susceptibility.
OBJECTIVE: The purpose of this study was to evaluate visualization of CM using QSM, assess contrast between CM and adjacent nuclei, and indirectly compare across WMn and MP2RAGE.
METHODS: This retrospective study included patients with solitary cerebral cavernous malformations, not involving the thalamus, who underwent surveillance MRI including QSM (n=24). WMn sequences were obtained from a separate cohort of patients with epilepsy (n=16). MP2RAGE sequences were acquired from healthy individuals (n=24). All sequences were registered to the MNI152 template space and compared with the Morel histological atlas. Normalized intensity differences, contrast-to-noise ratios (CNR), and signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) were calculated for CM and neighboring nuclei.
RESULTS: On QSM, CM was hypointense to medial and posterior thalamus and hyperintense relative to motor thalamus. Median CNR on QSM (P<0.05) relative to CM was highest for medial pulvinar (median 2.9, interquartile range 1.6-4.7) and ventral lateral thalamus (1.6, 0.6-2.3). Highest overall CNR was seen on WMn for PuM (3.4, 3.0-4.0). SNR on QSM was highest for anterior pulvinar (2.4, 1.1-3.6) and highest overall SNR was on on MP2RAGE for PuA (20.8, 17.3-24.3). In an indirect comparison across independent cohorts, QSM showed greater lateral thalamic contrast than WMn and MP2RAGE, but lower overall SNR.
CONCLUSION: QSM allows visualization of CM including the lateral border poorly seen on other sequences, and may be useful as a complementary sequence for direct targeting of CM.

A.title: Polycythemia Vera Transforming to Pure Erythroid Leukemia: A Diagnostic Mimic of Thrombotic Microangiopathy With High-Risk TP53 Biology.
A.abstract: Leukemic transformation of polycythemia vera (PV) to acute myeloid leukemia (AML) with a predominantly erythroid blast population is rare and carries a poor prognosis, particularly when driven by a TP53 mutation. We report a 55-year-old man with JAK2 V617F-positive PV, previously noted on surveillance biopsy to harbor a TP53 mutation and Grade 2 marrow fibrosis, who presented three years later with pancytopenia, schistocytosis, hyperferritinemia, hypofibrinogenemia, and altered mental status. The initial clinical presentation raised concern for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), while the presence of rare circulating blasts and coagulopathy also prompted consideration of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APML). Empiric plasma exchange, corticosteroids, and all-trans retinoic acid were initiated. ADAMTS13 activity and PML-RARA FISH subsequently returned negative. The patient deteriorated with multiorgan failure and expired before leukemia-directed therapy could be initiated. Postmortem bone marrow results demonstrated greater than 90% erythroid blasts with TP53 protein overexpression, a TP53 p.C238Y mutation (VAF 66%), and a triploid karyotype with 7p and 19p abnormalities, consistent with pure erythroid leukemia (PEL) arising from an antecedent myeloproliferative neoplasm. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges posed by overlapping clinical features of TTP and APML, including limitations in immunophenotypic assignment of the erythroid lineage. Importantly, it provides a longitudinally documented example of a TP53 mutation detected three years before overt transformation and describes a previously unreported presentation mimicking both TTP and APML.

A.title: PANDAS in the post-COVID era: links to group A Streptococcus and implications for pediatric neuropsychiatry ‒ a narrative review.
A.abstract: Pediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorders associated with streptococcal infections (PANDAS) are defined by the abrupt onset of tics and/or obsessive-compulsive symptoms temporally linked to group A Streptococcus (GAS). Post-pandemic reports note a rebound of pediatric invasive GAS (iGAS), providing an epidemiologic backdrop for more frequent neuropsychiatric presentations. This narrative review (2020-2025; PubMed/MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, Wiley Online Library, MDPI, plus snowballing) synthesizes evidence on the PANDAS/PANS-GAS relationship, clinical spectrum, differential diagnosis with Sydenham chorea (SC), immunopathogenesis, and treatment. Beyond classic OCD and motor tics, the phenotype includes speech disfluency, ocular tics, and acute eating restriction with functional and nutritional risk. Immunologic data support molecular mimicry, Th17/IL-17-driven neuroinflammation, blood‒brain barrier dysfunction, and antineuronal or folate receptor-α antibodies; however, no single validated biomarker exists, and antistreptolysin O (ASO), anti-DNase B document exposure only. Management is individualized and multimodal: antibiotic eradication (with prophylaxis in selected, frequently relapsing cases), immunomodulation (steroids, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), therapeutic plasma exchange) for severe/refractory courses, and Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (CBT/SSRIs) for core psychiatric symptoms. Contemporary data strengthen a post-streptococcal, immune-mediated framework while underscoring heterogeneous case definitions and the paucity of high-quality trials; prospective biomarker and treatment validation remain priorities.

A.title: Navigating obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome: pathophysiology, diagnosis, and therapeutic advances.
A.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome (OAPS) is a complex autoimmune disorder that contributes significantly to pregnancy morbidity. Despite advances in understanding its mechanisms, 20-30% of women, especially those refractory to standard treatments, continue to face adverse outcomes. Emerging therapies, including biologics and immunomodulators, are under investigation; however, data in this field remain limited.
AREAS COVERED: This review examines the current understanding of OAPS pathogenesis and risk stratification. It evaluates established management strategies such as aspirin and heparin, and explores adjunctive or investigational therapies, including hydroxychloroquine, corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulins, statins, plasma exchange, and biologics. Key knowledge gaps, concerning refractory cases and personalized treatment approaches, are highlighted, emphasizing the importance of multidisciplinary, risk-based care throughout preconception, pregnancy, and postpartum. This review focuses primarily on primary OAPS rather than secondary APS associated with systemic lupus erythematosus.
EXPERT OPINION: Innovations in immunotherapy and targeted biologics hold promise for refractory OAPS; however, large trials are needed to confirm their safety and efficacy during pregnancy. Future management is likely to involve biomarker-driven strategies, incorporating machine learning to enhance prediction and individualization of treatment. The development of standardized diagnostic criteria and risk assessment tools, alongside multidisciplinary collaboration, will be crucial in advancing care, ultimately transforming maternal-fetal health outcomes.

A.title: Tandem Extracorporeal Blood Purification/Support Therapies in Critically Ill Children: A Literature Review.
A.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the current evidence, clinical indications, methodologies, outcomes, and challenges associated with tandem extracorporeal blood purification/support therapies (EBP/STs) in critically ill children.
DATA SOURCES: A literature review of peer-reviewed articles, clinical guidelines, and existing literature related to continuous renal replacement therapy, therapeutic plasma exchange, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and their concurrent use in critically ill children.
STUDY SELECTION: Studies were included if they described tandem use of EBP/ST modalities in children, including case series, observational studies, and expert reviews. Studies focusing exclusively on adult populations or single modality therapy were excluded.
DATA EXTRACTION: Key data points extracted were patient population, clinical indication for tandem therapy, type and sequence of EBP/ST modality used, reported outcomes, and complications. Emphasis was placed on child-specific applications, safety profiles, and treatment protocols.
DATA SYNTHESIS: Tandem EBP/ST are increasingly used to treat children with complex conditions such as sepsis-induced multiple organ failure, acute liver failure, and thrombocytopenia-associated multiple organ dysfunction syndrome. This review synthesizes the reported risks, benefits, and proposed protocols for tandem therapy use in PICUs. Benefits include reduced procedural downtime, optimized vascular access, and enhanced therapeutic efficiency. However, tandem therapies remain off-label, with widely variable clinical protocols, lack of children-specific guidelines, and increased risk of complications such as hypocalcemia and hemodynamic instability, limiting their widespread adoption.
CONCLUSIONS: Tandem EBP/STs remain an emerging but incompletely standardized intervention in pediatric critical care. While they offer potential benefits such as improved procedural efficiency and reduced vascular access requirements, their use is limited by heterogeneous protocols, off-label application, and risk of complications. Efforts toward developing standardized guidelines, enhancing multidisciplinary training, and establishing multicenter registries may help optimize their safe and effective use in critically ill children.

A.title: Myasthenia Gravis - An Updated Review.
A.abstract: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction (NMJ) disorder characterized by fatigable weakness in skeletal and ocular muscles. The etiology is the presence of autoimmune antibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors (AChR) or other muscle-specific proteins. The result is muscle end plate dysfunction and weakness. While symptoms may be limited to ocular muscles (ocular MG/OMG), systemic generalization of symptoms (generalized MG/gMG) can frequently occur. Diagnosis relies on a history of fluctuating weakness, diurnal variation in muscle strength, physical examination signs of fluctuating muscle weakness, supported by serology and electrophysiologic studies. In its most severe form, called myasthenic crisis, weakness can involve respiratory muscles, and can cause life-threatening hypoxemia needing critical care monitoring and invasive ventilation. Management of MG is multimodal and may need a combination of acetyl cholinesterase inhibitors, immunomodulators such as steroids, and steroid-sparing agents, intravenous agents, such as intravenous immunoglobulin, or plasma exchange, rarely needing surgical options such as thymectomy. Recent advances have added novel therapeutics as viable treatment options.

A.title: A Chiral Virus-Like Nanoplatform That Broadly Mediates Antibiotic Delivery to the Brain for Bacterial Meningitis Therapy.
A.abstract: Blood-brain barrier (BBB) preserves brain homeostasis yet restricts therapeutics; in bacterial meningitis, antibiotics' limited penetration impairs delivery to the parenchyma and cerebrospinal fluid, constraining efficacy and motivating strategies to overcome the barrier. To address this, we developed a chiral virus-mimicking mesoporous silica nanostructure (CVSN) functionalized with L-alanine for antibiotic delivery. It offers several distinct advantages: (1) nanoscale dimensions facilitating BBB transport; (2) virus-like morphology enhancing vascular accumulation and penetration, providing a foundation for passive targeting; (3) chiral surface modification conferring active recognition capacity for more efficient biological targeting; and (4) a mesoporous architecture that ensures high drug-loading efficiency and controlled release of drugs. Experimentally, it achieves efficient BBB penetration into the brain parenchyma and shows targeted delivery into microglia and astrocytes. Simulating the loading of cargoes by viruses, it ultimately improves the bioavailability and brain parenchyma and cerebrospinal fluid contents of various antibiotics with distinct physicochemical properties, antibacterial spectrum, and BBB penetration capacity, including cefoperazone, norfloxacin, levofloxacin and imipenem. It helps to treat meningitis induced by both Gram-negative bacteria (e.g., Escherichia coli) and Gram-positive bacteria (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus) and provides a promising avenue to overcome the limitations imposed by the BBB for CNS infections antibiotic therapy in clinic.

A.title: NECTIN-4 orchestrates macrophage-mediated tumor plasticity in oral squamous cell carcinoma.
A.abstract: Tumor associated macrophages (TAM) are key regulator of the tumor microenvironment (TME), however, the upstream factors that contribute to the polarization and functional reprogramming in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remain largely unclear. This study evaluates the role of Nectin-4 in modulating tumor-immune interactions and its impact on OSCC progression. Detailed transcriptomic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)-OSCC dataset revealed that high NECTIN-4 expression was associated with enrichment of pathways involved in epithelial mesenchymal transition (EMT), angiogenesis, and stemness, and was inversely correlated with inflammatory signaling and immune infiltration.Additionally, single-cell transcriptomic analyses demonstrated an increase in macrophages, solely focused on the stroma, in Nectin-4 high tumors. Consistently, SCC-9 cells exhibited high levels of Nectin-4 and Nectin-4 enriched conditioned media (CM) derived from SCC-9 cells induced polarization of THP-1 monocytes toward a TAMs-like phenotype, characterized by increased CD163 expression and elevated secretion of immunomodulatory cytokines such as CCL-2. Co-culture of TAMs with SCC-9 cells promoted tumor aggressiveness, as evidenced by increased expression of EMT markers (E-cadherin, N-cadherin, vimentin) and stem cell markers (CD133, OCT4), invasion and cytoskeletal remodeling. These TAMs also enhanced angiogenesis in cancer cells by increasing the expression of VEGF-A, angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1), and TGF-β, along with in ovo neovascularization and promoting endothelial tube formation. Overall, the study identifies Nectin-4 as a key mediator of tumor-immune crosstalk in OSCC, driving macrophage enrichment, immune suppression and pro-tumorigenic signaling. Therefore, targeting Nectin-4 signaling could be a new approach to restore anti-tumor immunity and inhibit OSCC progression.

A.title: The role of nanomedicine in infectious diseases of the central nervous system: a narrative review.
A.abstract: Infectious diseases in the central nervous system (CNS) are a global health problem, causing significant morbidity and mortality. One of the main challenges in treating CNS infections is the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which limits drug delivery to the brain. During infections, brain-resident immune cells, release inflammatory mediators, which further contribute to neuroinflammation and damage. Nanomedicine offers an alternative for CNS treatment that has been explored in several types of infections. Across preclinical studies, nanomedicine approaches have demonstrated substantial improvements in CNS delivery and therapeutic outcomes, including reductions in brain pathogen burden of up to 3 log10 colony-forming units, increases in brain drug concentrations of 3-4-fold, and survival improvements of up to 100% in selected infection models. However, the literature remains fragmented across pathogens, nanomaterial platforms, and experimental models, with few direct comparisons and limited clinical validation. This review provides a comprehensive, up-to-date synthesis of the current evidence, integrating emerging nanomedicine strategies across major CNS infections while highlighting common therapeutic approaches, clinical applications, limitations, and key gaps that must be addressed to advance these technologies toward clinical translation. It also highlights advances and techniques in nanomedicine for treating brain infections, discusses clinical applications, and promotes innovation and future directions.

A.title: Single-Cell Multiomics Integration Reveals Cell Trajectories and Regulatory Networks in Breast Cancer Progression.
A.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Breast cancer is a molecularly heterogeneous disease encompassing distinct subtypes with divergent prognoses and therapeutic responses. Despite extensive bulk genomic characterization, the single-cell transcriptional trajectories, chromatin regulatory landscapes, and intercellular communication networks that drive breast cancer progression from luminal to mesenchymal states remain incompletely understood. Emerging evidence implicates gut microbiome dysbiosis as a systemic modulator of breast cancer risk, immune regulation, and treatment response; however, its coordinated characterization alongside high-resolution single-cell profiling has not been undertaken. Integrating single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with chromatin accessibility profiling (scATAC-seq), cell-cell communication inference, and gut microbiome 16S rRNA analysis offers a comprehensive multilayered approach to dissecting both the intratumoral regulatory logic and the systemic microbial landscape of breast cancer progression.
METHODS: We performed integrated multiomics analysis of 42,037 high-quality single cells from breast cancer patient samples obtained from the GEO database (GSE161529), encompassing tumor and adjacent normal tissue. scRNA-seq data were processed using Seurat v4.3.0 and Scanpy v1.9.1. Dimensionality reduction, Leiden clustering, differential expression analysis, pseudotime trajectory inference (Monocle3, scVelo, Slingshot), SCENIC regulon analysis, chromatin accessibility profiling, cell-cell communication inference (CellChat), and functional enrichment analysis were applied. Key marker genes were validated by quantitative RT-PCR in MCF-7 and MDA-MB-231 cell lines. In parallel, gut microbiome 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing data from 599 matched breast cancer-healthy control pairs (266 genera, four BioProjects) were analyzed for alpha/beta diversity, differential genus abundance (Mann-Whitney U with Benjamini-Hochberg correction), genus co-occurrence networks, and random forest breast cancer classification.
RESULTS: Unbiased clustering identified 12 observed cell populations spanning luminal (Luminal A, Luminal B), basal, HER2+, cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF), tumor-associated macrophage (TAM), CD8 T cell, regulatory T cell (Treg), NK cell, B cell, endothelial, and pericyte compartments. Quality control confirmed robust data quality with median 2400-3100 genes per cell and mitochondrial content below 20%. Pseudotime trajectory analysis revealed a continuous epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) spectrum with three divergent lineages: EMT, senescence, and immune activation branches. SCENIC identified SNAI1(+), ZEB1(+), and FOXM1(+) as the most differentially activated regulons in basal/mesenchymal cells. ATAC-seq chromatin accessibility profiling confirmed EMT transcription factor access through distal enhancers. CellChat identified TGF-β1-TGFBR1 (CAF → tumor) and PD-L1-PD-1 (tumor → CD8 T cell) as dominant intercellular communication axes. Multiomics integration enhanced cell-type classification AUC from 0.76 (scRNA-seq alone) to 0.91 (full multiomics). EMT-high tumor status was associated with significantly inferior overall survival (HR = 2.14, p = 0.001). qRT-PCR validation confirmed ERBB2 enrichment in HER2+ lines and KRT5/VIM enrichment in basal/TNBC lines (all p < 0.001). Gut microbiome analysis revealed significant dysbiosis in breast cancer patients versus healthy controls, with reduced Shannon diversity (1.94 vs. 2.06, p = 6.1 × 10-4), significant community-level separation (Bray-Curtis PERMANOVA F = 30.2, p = 0.001), and nine differentially abundant genera including enriched Faecalitalea (log2 F C = 1.44), Parasutterella (log2 F C = 1.21), and Bacteroides (log2 F C = 1.19). A random forest microbiome classifier achieved a cross-validated AUC of 0.79 (95% CI: 0.74-0.82), supporting the gut-breast axis as a systemic codeterminant of cancer state.
CONCLUSIONS: This integrated single-cell multiomics and gut microbiome atlas of breast cancer progression characterizes the transcriptional regulatory architecture driving cellular trajectory diversification, highlights SNAI1-ZEB1-FOXM1 coregulatory networks as candidate therapeutic targets, suggests that multiomics integration can enhance molecular stratification of breast cancer subtypes with clinical prognostic relevance, and identifies gut microbiome dysbiosis as a potential systemic dimension-characterized by loss of microbial diversity and enrichment of specific genera-as a systemic dimension of breast cancer pathobiology that warrants integration with intratumoral molecular profiling.

A.title: Laminar Wall Shear Stress in Brain Arteriovenous Malformations: Systematic Review of Literature.
A.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Laminar wall sheer stress (LWSS) modulates inflammatory activity of the endothelium and may be a contributing factor in many cerebrovascular pathologies. There is a lack of consensus whether significant differences in LWSS exist between feeding vessels in brain arteriovenous malformation (bAVM) and healthy vessels. A systematic review of LWSS research in bAVM was undertaken, including the methods used and the assumptions made in determining LWSS.
METHODS: Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Scopus electronic databases were systematically searched from inception for articles calculating LWSS in bAVM cases. LWSS values were extracted for comparison between ipsilateral bAVM feeding arteries and healthy contralateral vessels or healthy normative data.
RESULTS: Three retrospective cohort studies were identified, reporting on 42 adult and pediatric bAVM cases. Mean LWSS (mLWSS) in healthy vessels (contralateral vessels or normative controls) typically ranged from 1.2-2.7 Pa, while mLWSS values in untreated bAVM feeding arteries typically ranged from 1.6-3.6 Pa. All studies had mixed cohorts of ruptured and unruptured cases, obscuring the relationship between LWSS and bAVM history.
CONCLUSIONS: mLWSS values in healthy arteries and bAVM feeding vessels tend to be low and overlapping. Further research of high scientific and methodologic quality is necessary to improve understanding of how LWSS hemodynamics relate to bAVM formation, rupture, and treatment.

A.title: [Advances in the diagnosis and treatment of capillary malformation-arteriovenous malformation syndrome].
A.abstract: Capillary malformation-arteriovenous malformation (CM-AVM) syndrome is a rare hereditary vascular disorder encountered in clinical practice. Owing to its complex pathogenesis, heterogeneous clinical manifestations, and challenging diagnostic criteria, CM-AVM syndrome is frequently misdiagnosed or underdiagnosed clinically. Accumulating studies have demonstrated that CM-AVM syndrome is predominantly induced by mutations in the RASA1 and EPHB4 genes. Such genetic aberrations activate the Ras/MAPK signaling pathway, thereby driving the onset and progression of the disease. The primary clinical hallmark of CM-AVM syndrome is widespread multiple cutaneous capillary spots, which are often accompanied by deep-seated arteriovenous malformations that may trigger severe systemic complications. The definitive diagnosis of this syndrome relies on comprehensive integration of clinical manifestations, imaging findings, and genetic testing results. Current therapeutic strategies for CM-AVM syndrome include laser therapy, photodynamic therapy, targeted pharmacotherapy, and interventional surgery. This review systematically summarizes the latest research advances in the etiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, and management of CM-AVM syndrome, aiming to deepen the clinical understanding of this rare disease and provide evidence-based references for the optimization of individualized treatment regimens in future clinical practice.

A.title: The genetics of vascular anomalies.
A.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: To summarize clinically relevant findings in the genetic cause and gene expression of vascular anomalies.
RECENT FINDINGS: Infantile hemangioma demonstrates familial clustering and is associated with atopic disease. Variable gene expression is seen in infantile hemangioma during proliferation and involution. Capillary malformation may be sporadic or inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Capillary malformation-arteriovenous malformation is caused by mutation in RASA1. Some inherited forms of lymphedema are due to mutation in VEGFR3. Venous malformation may be sporadic, paradominant, or autosomal dominant inheritance. Autosomal dominantly inherited forms of venous malformation are due to mutations in TIE2/TEK. Additionally, TIE2 somatic mutations have been identified in about half of sporadic venous malformations.
SUMMARY: Multiple genes have been identified causing inherited forms of vascular anomalies including capillary malformations, venous malformations and lymphedema. Variable gene expression of infantile hemangioma during proliferation and involution may offer new therapeutic targets for treatment.

A.title: Partial Red Cell Exchange in the Secondary Prevention of Stroke in Sickle Cell Disease: A Prospective Study.
A.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Stroke is a severe complication associated with sickle cell disease (SCD). The risk of recurrence is extremely high. The present study aimed to assess the clinical and biological efficacy of Partial Red Cell Exchange (PRE) in secondary stroke prevention among a cohort of Tunisian patients with SCD.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: We conducted a prospective study over a 15-year period (January 1, 2010-December 31, 2024). A total of 29 patients with sickle cell syndromes complicated by one or more strokes were enrolled. They underwent 1732 PRE.
RESULTS: The median age was 99 months (75-133). The median follow-up duration was 78 months (49-126). The mean HbS decreased from 40.1% ± 14.1% to 21.1% ± 11.1% post-exchange (p < 0.0001). Treatment failure was observed in 8 of 29 patients (27.5%), with a total of 12 neurological events over a cumulative treatment duration of 1570 months. 11 of 12 recurrences (91.7%) occurred within the first 4 years of the exchange program. The presence of moyamoya vasculopathy was predictive of therapeutic failure.
CONCLUSIONS: PRE remains an effective modality for secondary stroke prevention in patients with sickle cell disease. Stroke recurrences occur predominantly within the first 4 years of treatment and are more frequent in the context of severe cerebrovascular disease.

A.title: Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis Thought to Be due to Undifferentiated Connective Tissue Disease Treated With Ruxolitinib: A Case Report.
A.abstract: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a life-threatening, systemic inflammatory syndrome. Cases without an identifiable acquired trigger are referred to as secondary HLH. In this report, we describe the case of a 24 year-old woman whose underlying cause of HLH was particularly difficult to determine. Her condition was initially suspected to be due to lamotrigine use but is now thought to be a result of undifferentiated connective tissue disease. During the patient's prolonged and complex hospital stay, she received the diagnosis of secondary HLH. Discontinuing lamotrigine, a drug that rarely causes HLH, did not improve her condition. The patient was tested for infectious and malignant conditions with negative results. Further workup revealed a positive ANA and bilateral MCP tenosynovitis, with negative specific antibodies, suggesting an undefined rheumatologic process. A number of conventional therapies did not show clear benefit, including etoposide, high-dose steroids, rituximab, and plasmapheresis. The patient remained in critical condition until she began treatment with ruxolitinib, with which she remains stable more than 5 years later. Ruxolitinib has shown some success in treating HLH in preliminary studies, but it is still considered a salvage therapy. A.title: Ocular and Neuro-Ophthalmic Manifestations of Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy.
A.abstract: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) is an immune-mediated neuropathy characterized by demyelination and axonal injury of peripheral nerves. While its hallmark presentation involves progressive sensorimotor deficits, an underrecognized subset of patients develop ocular and neuro-ophthalmic manifestations. These include optic neuritis, optic atrophy, vision loss, ophthalmoplegia, extraocular muscle enlargement with proptosis, intracranial hypertension, and corneal small fiber pathology. Electrophysiologic and imaging studies, including visual evoked potentials, optical coherence tomography, and corneal confocal microscopy, have further revealed subclinical involvement of the optic nerve and retina, underscoring an expanded disease spectrum beyond classic peripheral neuropathy. The pathophysiology is multifactorial, involving demyelination, inflammatory cell infiltration, and immune-mediated axonal injury, with evidence suggesting potential central nervous system and cranial nerve involvement. These atypical manifestations often mimic disorders such as multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders, or thyroid eye disease, complicating early diagnosis. Importantly, most cases respond to standard immunomodulatory therapies, including intravenous immunoglobulin, corticosteroids, and plasma exchange. Advances in ocular imaging and biomarker discovery provide promising avenues for earlier detection and monitoring of neuro-ophthalmic involvement. Recognition of ocular features in CIDP is essential for timely diagnosis and treatment. Interdisciplinary collaboration between neurologists and ophthalmologists can prevent vision-threatening complications, refine diagnostic accuracy, and optimize long-term outcomes. Future studies are warranted to elucidate the mechanisms underlying ocular involvement and to evaluate emerging targeted therapies that may improve prognosis in these atypical but clinically significant phenotypes.

A.title: Autoimmune Optic Neuropathy: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Therapeutic Advances.
A.abstract: Autoimmune optic neuropathy (AON) encompasses a heterogeneous group of immune-mediated optic nerve inflammatory disorders, characterized by progressive or recurrent visual loss with or without optic disc edema, and distinct autoantibody profiles and neuroimaging features. This review synthesizes current knowledge on AON, highlighting key advances in the discovery of disease-specific biomarkers [eg, aquaporin-4 (AQP4)-IgG for NMOSD, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG)-IgG for MOG-associated disease (MOGAD), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP)-IgG for astrocytopathy], while neuroimaging and optical coherence tomography (OCT) aid subtype differentiation. Therapeutically, acute management relies on high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (IVMP), with plasma exchange for steroid-refractory cases; long-term maintenance is subtype-tailored. Prognosis varies by subtype, with MOG-ON showing better recovery than AQP4-ON, and CRMP5-IgG-associated ON carrying poor outcomes. Even with breakthroughs in pathogenetic understanding and targeted treatments, challenges reinforce the importance of continued interdisciplinary research to optimize AON management.

A.title: Glucocorticoid-free remission with simultaneous mepolizumab and rituximab in life-threatening PR3-ANCA-positive eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis: a case report and literature review.
A.abstract: Patients with features of multiple systemic vasculitides are rare but do exist and can be diagnostically challenging. In particular, it can be difficult to distinguish granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) with eosinophilia, proteinase 3 (PR3)-ANCA-positive eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), and overlap of GPA and EGPA in clinical practice. Nevertheless, in severe cases, rapid therapeutic decisions are required. We report such a life-threatening case of PR3-ANCA-positive vasculitis with eosinophilia, refractory to conventional therapy, that achieved remission with simultaneous biologic therapy using mepolizumab (MPZ) and rituximab (RTX) and provide a case-based review of the efficacy and safety of this dual biologic therapy. An 18-year-old man presented with cough, hemoptysis, leg purpura, and marked eosinophilia (4575/μL). Chest CT revealed alveolar hemorrhage (DAH). Proteinase 3 (PR3)-anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) was positive, and skin biopsy showed leukocytoclastic vasculitis with eosinophil infiltration, consistent with EGPA. He was refractory to methylprednisolone (mPSL) pulse therapy and intravenous cyclophosphamide (IVCY), and DAH worsened, requiring non-invasive ventilation. Plasma exchange, MPZ (300 mg), and RTX (375 mg/m2 weekly × 4) were administered. DAH resolved rapidly after MPZ administration. Eosinophils dropped to 0/μL, but PR3-ANCA remained positive, and thereafter, nephritis developed. At 3 months after disease onset, renal biopsy showed pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis with little eosinophil infiltration. Additional mPSL pulses induced remission, which was maintained with MPZ and RTX. PR3-ANCA turned negative, and proteinuria resolved within 12 months. Glucocorticoids (GCs) were discontinued after 2.5 years, with a Vascular Damage Index (VDI) of 0. No serious infections or adverse events occurred. Although the development of glomerulonephritis after normalization of eosinophil count and DAH remission suggested possible EGPA-GPA overlap, the absence of granulomatous features and the potential phenotypic shift under anti-IL-5 therapy supported a final diagnosis of PR3-ANCA-positive EGPA. In life-threatening situations, the priority should be to initiate agents effective across both entities rather than to delay treatment until classification is certain. Our review suggests that simultaneous biologic therapy with MPZ and RTX can be effective with minimal adverse events and should be considered without hesitation in such critical cases.

A.title: Decellularized Extracellular Matrix Hydrogel With Schwann Cell Conditioned Medium Accelerates Skin Wound Healing in Diabetic Mice.
A.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic nonhealing wounds represent a major complication of diabetes mellitus and impose a substantial clinical burden worldwide. Impaired reparative function of Schwann cells (SCs), along with the subsequent loss of paracrine repair signals, has been identified as a critical pathologic driver of delayed diabetic wound healing. Decellularized dermal matrix hydrogels have emerged as promising biomimetic platforms for local factor delivery and tissue regeneration. Nevertheless, the therapeutic potential of combining SC-derived conditioned medium with decellularized extracellular matrix hydrogels (dECMMA) for diabetic wound repair remains unexplored.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this study, a photocrosslinkable methacrylated porcine dermal dECMMA loaded with RSC96 SC conditioned medium (dECMMA@RC) was fabricated. The microstructure of the hydrogels was characterized through scanning electron microscopy. In vitro, cytocompatibility, cell proliferation, and migration were evaluated in L929 fibroblasts, and pro-angiogenic capacity was assessed using a human umbilical vein endothelial cell tube formation assay. In vivo, full-thickness skin wounds were established in streptozotocin-induced type 1 diabetic mice. Wound healing outcomes were systematically evaluated by gross observation, histologic staining, immunofluorescence, and quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction.
RESULTS: The dECMMA@RC hydrogel maintained a favorable porous microstructure and exhibited no obvious cytotoxicity. Compared with the control and pure dECMMA groups, dECMMA@RC significantly promoted L929 cell proliferation and migration, as well as capillary-like tube formation of human umbilical vein endothelial cells in vitro. In diabetic mice, dECMMA@RC treatment markedly accelerated wound closure, enhanced reepithelialization, and increased the number of regenerated hair follicles and sebaceous glands. Mechanistic analysis revealed that dECMMA@RC downregulated the mRNA levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor alpha), and upregulated the expression of angiogenic markers (CD31, VEGF-A) and neuroregenerative markers (growth associated protein 43, nerve growth factor) in wound tissues.
CONCLUSIONS: The dECMMA@RC composite hydrogel effectively accelerates diabetic wound healing through the synergistic effects of anti-inflammation, pro-angiogenesis, and neuroregeneration. This strategy provides a novel and feasible approach for the development of bioactive dressings for chronic diabetic wounds.

A.title: Green-synthesized Nanoparticles as Emerging Antidepressant and Anxiolytic Candidates: A Critical Review of Preclinical Evidence and Translational Prospects.
A.abstract: The high incidence of depression and anxiety disorders worldwide, with figures of depression > 300 million and anxiety > 264 million, poses a serious challenge to health and wellness. Treatment is still limited by existing pharmacotherapies with delayed onset, adverse side effects, poor entry into the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and resistance in approximately 30% of patients. Green-synthesized nanoparticles (NPs) obtained via phytochemicals, microorganisms, and biomolecules are a promising sustainable route for neurotherapeutic applications. This critical review explores preclinical studies on the antidepressant and anxiolytic effects of green NPs, discussing their underlying mechanisms, translatability, and safety concerns in the context of the period 2015-2025. A comprehensive literature search on green synthesis, nanoparticles, Depression, Anxiety and Neurobehavioral outcomes was conducted using the Boolean operator in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Evidence suggests that green NPs can facilitate both serotonergic and dopaminergic signal modulation, minimize neuroinflammation, recruit NFκB, activate antioxidant activity via the Nrf2/ HO-1 axis and induce neuroplasticity (Akt/CREB/BDNF axis). Their biogenic characteristics on the surface may enhance BBB transport and biocompatibility and reduce cytotoxicity and environmental persistence. However, there is still inadequate evidence regarding chronic toxicity, biodistribution, synthesis reproducibility, mechanistic validation and clinical evidence. Nano optimization by AI (as well as characterizing nanomaterials in a standardized manner), nanoinformatics and personalized nano-neuropharmacology in the future are required. Green NPs have promising therapeutic potential; however, this has mainly been demonstrated in preclinical studies.

A.title: Novel acylation modifications in cerebrovascular disease: Molecular mechanisms, crosstalk and therapeutic potential.
A.abstract: Secondary injury in cerebrovascular disease involves energy failure, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption and neurovascular unit dysfunction. Novel lysine acylations, including lactylation, succinylation, beta-hydroxybutyrylation and crotonylation, have emerged as interfaces through which metabolic changes in lactate, succinate, ketone bodies and short-chain acyl-CoA species are translated into transcriptional regulation and altered protein function. This review organizes the evidence according to a framework that links metabolic donors, writer and eraser enzymes, modification sites, cell types and disease stages. We distinguish relatively developed experimental evidence in acute ischemic stroke and cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury from limited findings in haemorrhage and predominantly exploratory evidence in chronic hypoperfusion and vascular cognitive impairment. Proteomic studies have identified 1003 lactylation sites across 469 proteins in rats subjected to cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury, although most sites have not undergone causal validation. Comparatively strong evidence has accumulated for sites or regulatory axes involving MeCP2, SOD2, NEK7, ACSL4, PLBD1 and ZO-1. Collectively, current findings indicate that the effects of a given acylation cannot be inferred from its global abundance because they depend on substrate function, cellular origin and the therapeutic window. Major limitations include insufficient site-specific causal evidence, difficulty in directly quantifying crosstalk among post-translational modifications, poor correspondence between animal models and clinical heterogeneity and the absence of effective delivery systems and pharmacodynamic biomarkers. Future studies should integrate spatiotemporally resolved multi-omics, endogenous site editing, cell-specific models, measurable target engagement and independent clinical cohorts to evaluate whether selected acylation sites can progress from experimental candidates to independently validated clinical markers or intervention targets.

A.title: Pericytes as targets in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia.
A.abstract: Defective paracrine Transforming Growth Factor-β (TGF-β) signaling between endothelial cells and the neighboring mural cells have been thought to lead to the development of vascular lesions that are characteristic of Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT). Our recent findings have provided exciting insights into the role of thalidomide, a drug that reduces both the frequency and the duration of epistaxis in individuals with HHT by targeting mural cells. These advances provide opportunities for the development of new therapies for vascular malformations.

A.title: Droplet digital PCR as a first-line detection tool in the genetic diagnosis of vascular anomalies.
A.abstract: Targeted precision therapies are increasingly used in the treatment of individuals with vascular anomalies (VAs). This increases the need for rapid, accurate and inexpensive genetic diagnosis. Droplet digital polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR) is an alternative to next-generation sequencing (NGS), permitting rapid, highly sensitive interrogation of recurrent pathogenic mosaic variants. We examined the feasibility of ddPCR as a primary diagnostic tool in a large cohort of individuals with VAs. Lesional tissue was collected for ddPCR of up to 46 recurrent pathogenic variants across 16 genes associated with VAs. Specimens were assessed on a subset of assays for each individual based on clinical phenotype. Most individuals who had negative ddPCR results went on to high-depth gene panel or deep exome NGS, or Sanger sequencing. Here we report the phenotypic and molecular findings for 78 newly recruited and tested individuals in addition to the 60 individuals already reported from our cohort. The overall diagnostic yield for our cohort when combined with individuals previously reported was 104/138 (75%). Of 138 individuals tested, recurrent pathogenic variants were detected in 71 (51%) on ddPCR. Variants were most frequently identified in PIK3CA (n = 28), TEK (n = 18), GNAQ (n = 12), or MAP2K1 (n = 7). In a further 33 individuals, pathogenic variants were identified on NGS or Sanger sequencing. Our findings indicate that ddPCR is an efficient method achieving a high diagnostic yield in our cohort when used prior to sequencing.

A.title: Effective combined immunotherapy for severe hemolytic disease of the fetus.
A.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Maternal anti-Kell and anti-Rhesus D-alloimmunization cause severe hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDF) by crossing the placenta, leading to anemia and hydrops fetalis. Early-onset HDF from anti-K and anti-RhD alloimmunization often requires multiple, early intrauterine transfusions (IUTs), with higher complication rates and decreased sensitivity after the first intervention. Mortality remains high.
CASE REPORT: We report the successful treatment of three pregnant women with high-titer red cell alloantibodies-two with anti-K and one with anti-RhD-during the first trimester, a period with otherwise limited therapeutic options. We applied a novel triple therapy consisting of immunoadsorption (IA), high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and rituximab (Rtx) (IIR). This approach resulted in a marked reduction of antibody titers: anti-D decreased from 1:1024 to 1:16, and anti-K from 1:8192 and 1:2048 to 1:32, respectively. One patient presented at 19 weeks of gestation with fetal hydrops, severe anemia, and thrombocytopenia. IIR reduced the need for invasive procedures (intrauterine transfusions) and led to resolution of fetal thrombocytopenia. In the remaining two high-risk cases, IIR prevented the onset of fetal anemia. All neonates were delivered healthy and without anemia.
CONCLUSION: This case series presents a novel, safe personalized prophylactic and therapeutic approach that may delay anemia onset and reduce invasive procedures in high-risk patients with limited options and resulted in healthy neonates without apparent comorbidities.

A.title: [Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia - Bridging the Care Gap in the Early Neonatal Period].
A.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Kernicterus resulting from excessive bilirubin concentrations can be effectively prevented by early diagnosis and therapy. The postnatal rise of bilirubin peaks at a time of life most newborn infants have been discharged home while the next scheduled well baby visit is several weeks ahead.
AIM: Evaluating a post-discharge bilirubin follow-up program established in 2010.
METHODS: Retrospective analysis of newborns seen 2010-2024 at the Berlin University Medical Center bilirubin outpatient clinic, exchange transfusions performed in the same time period, and infants admitted for phototherapy in 2022.
RESULTS: The median annual number of infants consulting the outpatient clinic was 616 in 2010-2016, as compared to 1858 in 2017-2024. In 2022, 6% of newborns seen at the outpatient clinic were admitted for treatment of hyperbilirubinemia at a median age of 6 [5-7] days, with a total serum bilirubin concentration of 20.5 [19.3-21.4] mg/dl). The 2 top indications for the 81 exchange transfusions performed in 78 patients were rhesus incompatibility (n=44; 56%) and gestational alloimmune liver disease (n=24; 31%). The bilirubin level immediately prior to exchange transfusion was 15.5 [12.5-20.0] mg/dl (highest measured value 38.1 mg/dl).
CONCLUSION: A post-discharge program attached to a neonatal unit can effectively bridge the gap in care between discharge and scheduled well-baby visits several weeks ahead. A mandatory U2a could standardize follow-up care for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia in the future.

A.title: Refractory Anti-HMGCR Necrotizing Myopathy With Progressive Hypercapnic Respiratory Failure Responsive to a JAK Inhibitor.
A.abstract: Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) associated with 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (HMGCR) antibodies is a rare condition often associated with statin use. It typically presents with proximal weakness and markedly elevated creatine phosphokinase (CPK) levels and is often refractory, requiring long-term immunotherapy. Respiratory involvement is uncommon but can be life-threatening. Herein, we report the case of a 73-year-old woman with long-standing anti-HMGCR antibody-positive IMNM, refractory to glucocorticoids, methotrexate, azathioprine, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg), rituximab, and plasma exchange (PLEX), who presented with progressive hypercapnic respiratory failure. Despite ongoing treatment with IVIg, PLEX, and high-dose glucocorticoids, the patient's respiratory function worsened, and she required mechanical ventilation (MV). The addition of tofacitinib, a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor, coincided with marked clinical improvement, discontinuation of MV, and successful transition to room air. The patient continued to do well on this therapy, with improvement in muscle strength until outpatient discharge. The clinical benefit of JAK inhibition has been reported in dermatomyositis, overlap myositis, and anti-MDA5-positive disease, particularly in refractory cases with pulmonary or systemic involvement-but has not been described in the setting of refractory IMNM. In our patient, who had exhausted multiple conventional therapies and PLEX, the rapid clinical improvement after JAK inhibition strongly suggests a therapeutic effect and highlights the need for future studies of JAK inhibitors in IMNM.

A.title: Sevoflurane-associated diffuse alveolar hemorrhage: A rare cause of postoperative dyspnea. Case report and literature review.
A.abstract: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) is a rare, life threatening, early post-operative pulmonary complication of inhaled anesthetics, which are used for induction and maintenance of general anesthesia. It refers to hemorrhage originating from pulmonary microcirculation. It presents with hemoptysis, anemia, diffuse lung infiltration, and acute respiratory failure. Common causes are systemic vasculitis, Collagen vascular disease, Bone marrow transplantation, Drugs, and idiopathic conditions. Treatment ranges from supportive care and withdrawal of offending drugs to high-dose steroids, immunosuppressants, and plasmapheresis. Sevoflurane induced diffuse alveolar hemorrhage is a rarely reported entity in the literature that clinicians should be aware of and consider among the post-operative causes of dyspnea while ruling out other etiologies. We present a literature review over sevoflurane induced diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and a case involving a young otherwise healthy patient who underwent surgery for metatarsal fractures under general anesthesia, but diffuse alveolar hemorrhage developed after sevoflurane inhalation in the postoperative period.

A.title: Therapeutic Plasma Exchange in Pediatric Patients: A Multi-Institutional Landscape Analysis.
A.abstract: Pediatric evidence for therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) is largely small, single-center cohorts; there is no prior large-scale age-stratified outcomes assessment. Using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network, we identified 3744 patients ≤ 17 years old undergoing an index TPE procedure, stratified into four age groups (≤ 1, 2-5, 6-12, and 13-17 years). ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes recorded 30 days prior to the index procedure were mapped to American Society for Apheresis Categories I-III indications; three high-prevalence nonspecific codes were tracked separately. All-cause mortality at 30 days, 90 days, and 1 year was assessed. All-cause mortality decreased with increasing age at every time window: 30-day mortality ranged from 16.8% (≤ 1 year) to 4.3% (13-17 years, p < 0.0001). Infant mortality risk was concentrated disproportionately in the first 90 days postprocedure. Sex distribution shifted from a slight male predominance in infancy and early childhood (55%-56% male) to a female predominance in adolescence (55% female, p < 0.0001). Leading specific indications were autoimmune encephalitis (10%), sepsis with multiorgan failure (9%), renal transplant rejection (6%), acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (5%), Guillain-Barré syndrome (5%), and myasthenia gravis (4%); nonspecific diagnosis codes were each individually more prevalent than any single ASFA-mapped indication. This is the first large-scale, age-stratified, multi-institutional characterization of pediatric TPE. We identified an inverse relationship between age and all-cause mortality, a sex-distribution shift in adolescence, and an indication landscape dominated by nonspecific diagnosis codes. These findings offer age-stratified benchmarks for clinical counseling and hypothesis generation.

A.title: Cinchonidine Ameliorates Traumatic Brain Injury-Related Neurobehavioral Deficits via the SRC/RAF1/NF-κB Pathway to Attenuate Mitochondrial Dysfunction.
A.abstract: Cinchonidine (CD), a metabolite derived from gut microbiota, shows promise in protecting against traumatic brain injury (TBI), where mitochondrial dysfunction is a key driver of secondary damage. Using a mouse model of controlled cortical impact (CCI) and an in vitro primary neuron injury model, CD administration resulted in improved physiological status (weight recovery, stabilized heart rate) and behavioral outcomes (increased travel distance and speed) in TBI mice. Histological analysis showed reduced hippocampal neuronal damage, decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines (interleukin‑1β, interleukin‑6, and tumor necrosis factor‑α), and upregulated blood-brain barrier tight-junction proteins (Claudin-5, Occludin, zonula occludens‑1). Mitochondrial function was improved, evidenced by increased mitochondrial DNA copy number, elevated expression of translocase of outer mitochondrial membrane 20 and cytochrome c oxidase subunit IV, and restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential. In addition, CD attenuated TBI-induced changes in mitochondrial dynamics and biogenesis, restoring the phosphorylated dynamin-related protein 1 (p-DRP1)/DRP1 ratio and the expression of mitofusin 1/2 (MFN-1/2) and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α), while reducing mitochondrial DRP1. Network pharmacology identified proto‑oncogene tyrosine‑protein kinase Src (SRC) as a key target, validated by stable binding in molecular docking and drug affinity responsive target stability assays. Furthermore, cellular thermal shift assays demonstrated a direct interaction between CD and SRC. CD treatment suppressed the activation of the SRC/RAF proto-oncogene serine/threonine-protein kinase (RAF1)/nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) signaling axis, as evidenced by reduced phosphorylation of SRC and p65, along with decreased expression of RAF1 and cleaved Caspase-3. Crucially, SRC knockdown mimicked CD's protection, while SRC overexpression abolished its benefits. These findings suggest that CD ameliorates post-TBI mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and neuronal damage by inhibiting SRC kinase activity and its downstream RAF1/NF-κB signaling pathway. Thus, CD may represent a promising SRC-targeted neuroprotective strategy for TBI.

A.title: Bidirectional Regulatory Mechanisms of T cell-microglia Interactions in Cerebral Ischemic Disease: Molecular Crosstalk, Experimental Techniques and Therapeutic Implications.
A.abstract: Cerebral ischemic diseases, such as ischemic stroke (IS) and vascular dementia (VaD), are major causes of neurological disability and mortality. Neuroinflammation acts as a pivotal driver of secondary brain injury, mediated by intricate bidirectional interactions between peripheral T cells and central nervous system (CNS)-resident microglia. This review delineates the molecular mechanisms underlying T cell-microglia crosstalk in cerebral ischemia, emphasizing their dual roles in exacerbating neurotoxicity and promoting repair. Direct interactions involve antigen presentation via MHC-TCR engagement and co-stimulatory checkpoints (e.g., CD80/CD86-CD28, PD-L1-PD-1), which regulate T cell activation and microglial polarization. Direct signaling through cytokines (IFN-γ, IL-4, IL-17, IL-10) further modulates microglial phenotypes: Th1/Th17 cells drive pro-inflammatory M1 polarization via STAT1/NF-κB pathways, while Tregs/Th2 cells induce anti-inflammatory M2 states through STAT6/SMAD signaling. Spatial transcriptomics and single-cell omics reveal spatiotemporal dynamics of these interactions, identifying STAT1/STAT6 imbalance as a critical determinant of neuroinflammatory outcomes. Advanced methodologies, including two-photon intravital microscopy and microfluidic blood-brain barrier (BBB) models, enable real-time visualization of immune cell trafficking and synaptic communication. Therapeutically, targeting immune checkpoints (CTLA-4, PD-1) or cytokine pathways (e.g., IL-4 mimetics) shows promise in recalibrating neuroimmune responses. However, challenges such as blood-brain barrier impermeability to biologics and interspecies immune heterogeneity necessitate innovative delivery strategies. This review integrates molecular, cellular, and technological insights to propose a framework for precision immunomodulation. By elucidating context-dependent signaling nodes and leveraging emerging tools, the study underscores the potential of harnessing T cell-microglia crosstalk to mitigate neuroinflammation and enhance neural repair, offering transformative avenues for stroke and dementia therapy.

A.title: Mitochondrial Metabolic Reprogramming in Macrophages: A Key Driver of Rheumatoid Arthritis.
A.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by persistent synovitis and progressive cartilage and bone destruction. Synovial macrophages are central coordinators of inflammatory signaling, stromal activation, and osteoclastogenesis, yet their pathogenic functions cannot be explained by extracellular cytokine networks alone. Increasing evidence indicates that macrophage activation is coupled to cell-intrinsic mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming. Within the hypoxic, nutrient-variable, and inflammatory RA synovium, macrophages undergo coordinated changes in glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation, tricarboxylic acid cycle flux, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species production, fission-fusion dynamics, mitophagy, and mitochondrial DNA homeostasis. These alterations reshape bioenergetics while generating metabolites and organelle-derived danger signals that engage hypoxia-inducible factor 1α, nuclear factor-κB, the NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 inflammasome, and cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes signaling. The resulting metabolic-inflammatory circuits can stabilize pathogenic macrophage states and propagate inflammation to fibroblast-like synoviocytes, endothelial cells, and osteoclast-lineage cells. This review integrates current evidence on macrophage heterogeneity, mitochondrial remodeling, and intercellular signaling in RA. We further evaluate mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, metabolic modulation, restoration of mitochondrial quality control, inhibition of mitochondrial danger-signal sensing, and multistage nanodelivery. Particular emphasis is placed on evidence strength, macrophage-subset specificity, and the distinction between disease-driving abnormalities and compensatory adaptations. Finally, we outline the biomarkers, human-tissue validation, spatial multi-omics, and delivery strategies required to translate macrophage mitochondrial immunometabolism into precision therapy for RA.

A.title: Current concepts of vascular anomalies.
A.abstract: The field of vascular anomalies is confusing because numerous types of lesions exist, different anomalies often look similar, and imprecise terminology commonly is used. Pharmacotherapy is effective for certain vascular tumors; sclerotherapy generally is the primary treatment of problematic lymphatic and venous malformations. Arteriovenous malformations remain difficult to manage because of their high progression and recurrence rates. Propranolol has gained popularity recently for the treatment of problematic infantile hemangioma, but its efficacy and safety compared with corticosteroid therapy have not been studied. Continuing education is needed to increase the use of accepted biologic terms to describe vascular anomalies; this will improve patient care and facilitate research. As vascular anomalies centers continue to develop, children will have easier access to interdisciplinary expertise. Patients are most likely to be diagnosed and treated properly when managed by a specialist or team focused on these conditions. Recent insight into the etiopathogenesis of infantile hemangioma and vascular malformations may lead to novel therapies for these lesions in the near future.

A.title: Maternal immunoglobulin G anti-A and anti-B antibody titres for predicting neonatal immune sensitisation in ABO-incompatible pregnancies: The Maternal Anti-A and Anti-B Antibody Titres in ABO-Incompatible Pregnancies study.
A.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Maternal immunoglobulin G (IgG) anti-A and anti-B antibodies can cross the placenta and cause ABO haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn (ABO-HDFN). We aimed to evaluate whether maternal IgG anti-A and anti-B titres predict neonatal direct antiglobulin test (DAT) positivity in ABO-incompatible pregnancies.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this prospective observational cohort study, 889 consecutive ABO-incompatible mother-newborn pairs were enrolled between November 2025 and June 2026. Maternal IgG anti-A and anti-B titres were measured after 0.01 M dithiothreitol treatment using the conventional tube antiglobulin titration method. Neonatal ABO grouping and DAT were performed by column agglutination technology. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis and multivariable logistic regression assessed the predictive performance of maternal antibody titres.
RESULTS: Overall, 112/889 (12.6%) neonates were DAT positive. Maternal IgG anti-A and anti-B titres were significantly higher in mothers of DAT-positive neonates (both p < 0.001). Maternal IgG anti-A (area under the curve [AUC] 0.778) and anti-B (AUC 0.803) showed acceptable diagnostic performance. Higher thresholds (anti-A ≥32; anti-B ≥16) achieved 100% specificity, whereas lower thresholds (anti-A ≥8; anti-B ≥4) provided high sensitivity for excluding neonatal DAT positivity. Increasing maternal IgG anti-A (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.12, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.06-1.18) and anti-B titres (aOR 1.18, 95% CI: 1.09-1.28) independently predicted DAT positivity (both p < 0.001). Most DAT-positive neonates required phototherapy (94.6%) but none required exchange transfusion.
CONCLUSION: Standardised maternal IgG anti-A and anti-B titres independently could predict neonatal DAT positivity. A dual-threshold approach may complement existing antenatal assessment by identifying high-risk pregnancies and guiding individualised postnatal surveillance.

A.title: Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy in Acute Liver Failure: Rationale, Evidence, and Evolving Practice.
A.abstract: Acute liver failure (ALF) is a life-threatening condition hallmarked by an acute onset of liver dysfunction, coagulopathy, and encephalopathy in individuals without pre-existing liver disease. Advances in intensive care, coupled with increased access to liver transplant (LT), have substantially improved outcomes of individuals with ALF. Aggressive goal-directed intensive care focusing on individual organs has become the cornerstone of ALF management. In this context, continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) has emerged as a critical component in the management of ALF. While traditionally centered around providing renal support and optimizing renal injury, the use of CRRT in ALF has expanded to include potential benefits in controlling intracranial hypertension, managing volume status and metabolic abnormalities, and reducing hyperammonemia. The use of CRRT for nonrenal ALF-centric indications has gradually gained credence. This review examines the mechanistic aspects and principles of CRRT in ALF, summarizing current clinical evidence and practice patterns. We delve into aspects of basic circuit knowledge, timing of initiation, targets of therapy, challenges of anticoagulation, emerging literature on the combination of plasma exchange with CRRT, and provide insights into pragmatic decision-making with CRRT in ALF. Lastly, the review focuses on endpoints for the use of CRRT in ALF, as well as associated challenges and future directions.

A.title: Late-onset pneumocystis pneumonia after kidney transplantation: A systematic review and meta-analysis of prevalence, risk factors, and outcomes.
A.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Late-onset Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is increasingly recognized in kidney transplant recipients (KTRs) despite widespread prophylaxis. However, its prevalence and risk factors remain unclear.
METHODS: We systematically searched electronic databases for studies published up to May 1, 2025, that reported prevalence or risk factors of late-onset PCP. Pooled prevalence, weighted mean differences (WMDs), and pooled odds ratios (ORs) were synthesized using a random-effects model.
RESULTS: Of 1448 studies screened, 24 met inclusion criteria, comprising 57,662 KTRs, of whom 556 developed late-onset PCP. The pooled prevalence was 1.28 % (95 %CI 0.90-1.65). Lymphocyte counts were significantly lower in the infection group (WMD -408.34 cells/μL; 95 %CI -706.03 to -110.66). Risk was significantly increased with ABO-incompatible transplantation (OR 4.12; 95 %CI 1.04-16.30), rituximab induction (OR 4.77; 95 %CI, 1.50-15.21), corticosteroid (OR 2.56; 95 %CI 1.00-6.52) or mammalian target of rapamycin inhibitor (mTORi) maintenance (OR 2.37; 95 %CI 1.27-4.42), CMV infection (OR 5.21; 95 %CI 2.45-11.10), and rejection episodes (OR 2.93; 95 %CI 1.72-4.99), particularly when treated with plasma exchange, intravenous methylprednisolone, or rituximab. In contrast, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis reduced risk (OR 0.06; 95 %CI 0.01-0.60). Late-onset PCP was associated with graft loss (OR 6.11; 95 %CI 2.98-12.55) and mortality (OR 10.48; 95 %CI 1.92-57.16).
CONCLUSIONS: Although uncommon, late-onset PCP in KTRs is strongly linked with ABO-incompatible transplantation, lack of cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, lymphopenia, CMV infection, corticosteroid and mTORi, and rejection. KTRs with these high-risk features, including those receiving mTORi and corticosteroid maintenance, should be considered for prolonged or life-long PCP prophylaxis.

A.title: Innovations to Improve Survival in Acute Liver Failure.
A.abstract: Acute liver failure (ALF) is a medical emergency with high mortality rates. Liver transplantation is the optimal treatment for eligible patients. However, it necessitates access to transplantation services, significant financial resources, and frequently poses challenges in ensuring safe transportation. Advances in intensive care have improved survival rates from 20% to over 60%. Key factors include early prognostication, dynamic modeling, neurocritical monitoring, and liver support systems. There is a significant need for better public health services for preventing and managing ALF in India, highlighting the importance of innovative healthcare delivery and algorithm-based care. Recent advancements in liver support systems, novel pharmacological approaches, and enhanced critical care protocols can improve transplant-free survival in ALF. Innovative strategies like early and accessible plasma exchange (PLEX) for rodenticide poisoning-related ALF in Tamil Nadu have offered hope for improving public health services to provide innovative therapeutics in resource-constrained settings. This comprehensive review aims to explore the latest advancements in the management of ALF covering pathobiology, prognostic scores and biomarkers, noninvasive monitoring of intracranial hypertension (optic nerve sheath diameter and transcranial Doppler) and the use of modalities such as PLEX, and continuous renal replacement therapy. We highlight advancements and explore future innovations to enhance outcomes for individuals with ALF. Additionally, we address epidemiological changes in ALF in India and the associated challenges for healthcare policy.

A.title: Recent Progress in Double Filtration Plasmapheresis.
A.abstract: Double-filtration plasmapheresis is an advanced extracorporeal blood purification technique that selectively removes pathogenic macromolecules based on molecular weight. Unlike conventional plasma exchange, double-filtration plasmapheresis uses a two-step filtration process to retain beneficial plasma components such as albumin, while eliminating harmful substances, thereby reducing the need for exogenous plasma replacement. Over the last few decades, double-filtration plasmapheresis has gained prominence in the management of refractory autoimmune, neurological, metabolic, and renal diseases. This review systematically examines the therapeutic mechanisms, recent clinical advances, safety, limitations, and prospects of double-filtration plasmapheresis.

A.title: Analysis of multidimensional molecular mechanisms in Parkinson's disease and precise therapeutic strategies.
A.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), the second most common neurodegenerative disorder worldwide, is characterized by progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and striatal dopamine deficiency, leading to motor dysfunction. The complex pathogenesis involves impaired protein homeostasis with α-synuclein aggregation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation, including NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Newly identified regulated cell death pathways - including ferroptosis, cuproptosis, pyroptosis, and necroptosis - have further expanded current understanding of PD pathology, while gut-brain axis interactions may contribute to peripheral-central communication and disease progression. These mechanistic insights inspire targeted therapeutic strategies comprising α-synuclein inhibitors, mitochondrial protectants, anti-inflammatory agents, and novel cell death pathway blockers, alongside gut-brain axis interventions. However, these approaches face substantial challenges including limited blood-brain barrier penetration, insufficient target specificity, and individual genetic heterogeneity. Future research should prioritize developing multi-target combination therapies, integrating multi-omics and computational approaches for biomarker identification and patient stratification, while advancing clinical translation of gene- and cell-based therapies. Through interdisciplinary collaboration and precision medicine implementation, disease-modifying treatments for PD may become increasingly feasible.

A.title: Nanoparticle-Mediated Brain-Targeted Drug Delivery for Methamphetamine Use Disorder: Advances, Challenges and Translational Perspectives.
A.abstract: Methamphetamine use disorder (MUD) poses a significant global health challenge, lacking FDA-approved pharmacotherapies. Despite extensive exploration of therapeutic targets and interventions, effective treatment remains scarce due to challenges in delivering therapeutic agents to relevant brain regions at effective concentrations. Nanoparticle-mediated delivery offers a promising approach for transporting various therapeutic cargos to the central nervous system, including small molecules, nucleic acids, peptides, proteins, and gene-editing systems. However, the application of nanomedicine strategies in addressing the unique pathophysiological characteristics of MUD has not been systematically assessed. This review presents a problem-focused analysis of how lipid-based, polymeric, inorganic, biological, and hybrid nanocarriers tackle successive delivery obstacles such as systemic stability, blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, brain region-specific distribution, and controlled release of intracellular cargo. We compare preclinical nanotherapeutic approaches encompassing small-molecule neuroprotective agents, anti-METH vaccines, gene-silencing RNAs, neurotrophic proteins, and emerging gene-editing methods, outlining their respective benefits, limitations, and design considerations. Additionally, we explore key factors influencing nanomedicine performance in MUD, including protein corona formation, the impact of METH-related BBB dysfunction and neuroinflammation on nanoparticle distribution, and the disparity between acute animal models and chronic human MUD with relapse tendencies. In conclusion, we present a systematic framework for aligning nanocarrier characteristics with distinct delivery obstacles and therapeutic needs. We also emphasize forthcoming avenues such as disease-triggered nanocarriers, targeted delivery to specific regions, combined nanomedical approaches, theranostic strategies, and standardized assessments of biodistribution, effectiveness, safety, and translational potential.

A.title: Targeting NLRP3 Inflammasome Signaling After Myocardial Infarction: Mechanistic Rationale, Regulatory Networks, and Translational Perspectives.
A.abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) remains a major cause of death and heart failure despite advances in reperfusion and secondary prevention. Sterile inflammation triggered by ischemic myocardial injury is increasingly recognized as a determinant of infarct expansion, adverse ventricular remodeling, and subsequent clinical outcomes. The NOD-like receptor protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome integrates danger-associated molecular patterns, mitochondrial dysfunction, ionic disturbance, metabolic stress, and innate immune signaling. Following activation, caspase-1 processes interleukin-1β and interleukin-18 and cleaves gasdermin D to generate the pore-forming GSDMD-N fragment, thereby promoting pyroptosis and inflammatory amplification. After MI, NLRP3 activity is shaped by extracellular adenosine triphosphate and P2X7 signaling, potassium efflux, reactive oxygen species, mitochondrial DNA release, lysosomal and endoplasmic reticulum stress, and cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes signaling. Importantly, these responses are temporally and cell-type dependent: cardiomyocytes, macrophages, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts contribute differently to injury, debris clearance, vascular dysfunction, scar formation, and repair. This review differs from earlier pathway-centered summaries by integrating temporal regulation and cell-specific biology with emerging crosstalk among mitochondrial quality control, STING signaling, ferroptosis, pyroptosis, and immunometabolism. Translational evidence is considered alongside mechanism, including interleukin-1-directed studies such as CANTOS and the Virginia Commonwealth University Anakinra Remodeling Trial program, while emphasizing that clinical benefit from selective NLRP3 inhibition itself remains to be established. Direct inflammasome inhibitors, colchicine, metabolic modulators, RNA-based approaches, targeted delivery systems, and traditional Chinese medicine-derived compounds are critically discussed with attention to evidence level and limitations. We further examine biomarker-guided patient selection and unresolved questions concerning therapeutic timing, cell specificity, long-term safety, and preservation of reparative inflammation.
