B.title: Blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome: a case report and literature review.
B.abstract: Blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome (BRBNS) is a rare disease characterized by multiple venous malformations and hemangiomas in the skin and visceral organs. The lesions often involve the cutaneous and gastrointestinal systems. Other organs can also be involved, such as the central nervous system, liver, and muscles. The most common symptoms are gastrointestinal bleeding and secondary iron deficiency anemia. The syndrome may also present with severe complications such as rupture, intestinal torsion, and intussusception, and can even cause death. Cutaneous malformations are usually asymptomatic and do not require treatment. The treatment of gastrointestinal lesions is determined by the extent of intestinal involvement and severity of the disease. Most patients respond to supportive therapy, such as iron supplementation and blood transfusion. For more significant hemorrhages or severe complications, surgical resection, endoscopic sclerosis, and laser photocoagulation have been proposed. Here we present a case of BRBNS in a 45-year-old woman involving 16 sites including the scalp, eyelid, orbit, lip, tongue, face, back, upper and lower limbs, buttocks, root of neck, clavicle area, superior mediastinum, glottis, esophagus, colon, and anus, with secondary severe anemia. In addition, we summarize the epidemiology, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, differential diagnosis and therapies of this disease by analyzing all previously reported cases to enhance the awareness of this syndrome.

B.title: Vascular and perivascular lesions of skin and soft tissues in children and adolescents.
B.abstract: Vascular anomalies in children and adolescents are the most common soft tissue lesions and include reactive, malformative, and neoplastic tumefactions, with a full spectrum of benign, intermediate, and malignant neoplasms. These lesions are diagnostically challenging because of morphologic complexity and recent changes in classification systems, some of which are based on clinical features and others on pathologic findings. In recent decades, there have been significant advances in clinical diagnosis, development of new therapies, and a better understanding of the genetic aspects of vascular biology and syndromes that include unusual vascular proliferations. Most vascular lesions in children and adolescents are benign, although the intermediate locally aggressive and intermediate rarely metastasizing neoplasms are important to distinguish from benign and malignant mimics. Morphologic recognition of a vasoproliferative lesion is straightforward in most instances, and conventional morphology remains the cornerstone for a specific diagnosis. However, pathologic examination is enhanced by adjunctive techniques, especially immunohistochemistry to characterize the type of vessels involved. Multifocality may cause some uncertainty regarding the assignment of "benign" or "malignant." However, increased interest in vascular anomalies, clinical expertise, and imaging technology have contributed greatly to our understanding of these disorders to the extent that in most vascular malformations and in many tumors, a diagnosis is made clinically and biopsy is not required for diagnosis. The importance of close collaboration between the clinical team and the pathologist cannot be overemphasized. For some lesions, a diagnosis is not possible from evaluation of histopathology alone, and in a subset of these, a specific diagnosis may not be possible even after all assembled data have been reviewed. In such instances, a consensus diagnosis in conjunction with clinical colleagues guides therapy. The purpose of this review is to delineate the clinicopathologic features of vascular lesions in children and adolescents with an emphasis on their unique aspects, use of diagnostic adjuncts, and differential diagnosis.

B.title: Efficacy and safety of portable ultrasound-guided pingyangmycin sclerotherapy for deep-seated oral and maxillofacial venous malformations: a retrospective observational study.
B.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Intralesional sclerotherapy is the mainstay treatment for venous malformations (VMs). This study aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of ultrasound-guided pingyangmycin sclerotherapy for outpatients with deep-seated oral and maxillofacial VMs.
METHODS: This retrospective study included 49 outpatients with symptomatic deep-seated VMs in the oral and maxillofacial region who received portable ultrasound-guided pingyangmycin sclerotherapy between August 2023 and September 2025. The treatment response analysis after sclerotherapy included lesion volume reduction and symptom improvement. Ultrasound was used to calculate lesion volume. The assessment of global discomfort from the perspective of patients was calculated using the 0-10 numeric rating scale (NRS). The presence of complications was recorded during follow-up.
RESULTS: Among the 49 patients, the average number of sessions for each patient was 2 (range, 1-5). All patients experienced symptom relief after sclerotherapy. The median post-treatment NRS score was 0 (range, 0-1), compared with a median of 5 (range, 2-10) before sclerotherapy. Regarding lesion volume, twenty-one lesions (42.86%) demonstrated excellent response (≥90% reduction). Twenty-three lesions (46.94%) presented moderate response (≥50, <90% reduction). Five (10.2%) lesions showed mild reduction (<50% reduction). The mean lesion dimensions after treatments were 1.54 × 0.87 × 0.96 cm, with a corresponding calculated volume of 0.47 cm3, compared with average dimensions 3.27 × 1.69 × 1.85 cm (volume, 3.59 cm3) before sclerotherapy. A mean volume decrease of 82% was observed among all patients. Paired analysis showed significant improvement in both lesion volume and NRS score after the sclerotherapy. No severe complications occurred in this study.
CONCLUSION: Portable ultrasound-guided pingyangmycin sclerotherapy is a feasible and well-tolerated outpatient-based procedure for patients with deep-seated oral and maxillofacial venous malformations.

B.title: Management of spinal dural arterio-venous fistulas. Report of 12 cases and review of literature.
B.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Spinal cord arteriovenous malformations and fistulae are rare vascular lesions than can lead to myelopathy that is at many instances overlooked during diagnosing the cause of progressive myelopathy and weakness. This study aims to evaluate various treatment methods for sDAVFs and the outcome of these methods.
METHODS: This study involved 12 patients suffering from symptoms attributed to spinal dural arteriovenous fistulas; 11 were male and one was a female patient, with ages ranging between 50 years and 71 years. Good angiographic studies prior to treatment decision are a must, in order to plan the best approach according to the angioarchitecture of the fistula whether it will allow endovascular embolization or will surgery be more feasible.

B.title: A clinical study of pingyangmycin sclerotherapy for venous malformation: an evaluation of 281 consecutive patients.
B.abstract:
WHAT IS KNOWN AND OBJECTIVE: In China, lidocaine together with 2 mg/mL of pingyangmycin (PYM, also known as bleomycin A5) is recommended for the treatment of venous malformations (VMs). B.title: Treatment guidelines of lymphatic malformations of the head and neck.
B.abstract: Lymphatic malformations, traditionally called lymphangiomas, are diseases caused by development errors of the lymphatic system. About 90% of the cases occur within 2years of age, except a few cases which occur in adulthood, and approximately 75% of the lesions are located in the head and neck region. The lesions can grow rapidly with infection, trauma or bleeding, resulting in disfigurement as well as severe impairment of respiration, swallow and speech. Although lymphatic malformations are benign lesions, they rarely resolve spontaneously, their infiltrating nature coupled with the difficulty in distinguishing involved vital structures of head and neck from adjacent normal tissues makes complete surgical resection even more difficult. The likelihood of postsurgical recurrence and complications is thus higher than other vascular lesions. Surgical resection, sclerotherapy and laser therapy are currently the main treatment modes of lymphatic malformations. Various treatment options have their advantages and disadvantages, the selection of treatment modalities should depend on the patient's individual status and available technology and expertise. The treatment protocol should be individualized, comprehensive as well as sequential in order to obtain the best treatment outcome. Based on published literatures and clinical experiences, we devised the treatment guideline for management of head and neck lymphatic malformations. This protocol will be reviewed and updated periodically to include cutting edge knowledge to provide the best treatment options to benefit our patients.

C.title: Molecular Signatures of HIV-Induced Neuroinflammation and Neurodegeneration in Human Cerebral Organoids: Identification of Therapeutic Targets for NeuroHIV.
C.abstract: HIV-associated neurological complications remain a major concern in people living with HIV (PWH), even under effective viral suppression with combination antiretroviral therapy (cART), underscoring unresolved mechanisms driving HIV-related neurodegeneration. Microglia were preferentially infected and activated, initiating IL-17A-mediated cascades involving IFN-γ/STAT1, CEBPB, and NF-κB signaling. These pathways converged with cGAS-STING and Notch-NEURL1 signaling, both associated with neuroinflammation and synaptic dysfunction. cART suppressed viral replication, reduced IL-17A-mediated neuroinflammation, improved mitochondrial function, and restored synaptic gene expression. Collectively, these findings identify dysregulation of IL-17A, STAT1, CEBPB, and cGAS-STING signaling as key molecular drivers of HIV-associated neuroinflammation. They also establish a potential mechanistic link between IL-17A signaling and microglial remodeling, providing a translational framework for the development of CNS-targeted therapies in PWH.

C.title: Nifedipine-modulated gut microbiota attenuates hypertensive vascular injury through Bifidobacterium-associated inosine-Adora2b signaling.
C.abstract: Although antihypertensive drugs mitigate hypertensive vascular injury, their vascular benefits are not fully explained by blood pressure reduction alone. Many cardiovascular drugs reshape the gut microbiota, which in turn influences their vascular pharmacology. We therefore investigated whether gut microbiota remodeling contributes to nifedipine-mediated vascular protection in high-salt hypertensive rats and a pilot patient cohort. Combining 16S rRNA sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, fecal microbiota transplantation, microbiota depletion, supplementation, and selective receptor antagonism, we found that nifedipine ameliorated gut dysbiosis. Transplantation of nifedipine-modulated microbiota improved intestinal barrier integrity and reduced vascular inflammation, oxidative stress, collagen deposition, and vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) phenotypic switching, while only marginally lowering blood pressure. Conversely, microbiota depletion markedly attenuated these vascular benefits despite preserving nifedipine-induced blood pressure lowering. These vascular benefits were associated with nifedipine-restored Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis 420 (B420) and increased inosine availability. Supplementation with either recapitulated major vascular protective effects of nifedipine without statistically significant changes in blood pressure. In hypertensive patients, nifedipine treatment was associated with higher intestinal B420 abundance and inosine levels. In vitro, inosine modulated macrophages in an Adora2b- and Rap1-dependent manner, with accompanying changes in cAMP and KLF4, ameliorating VSMC dysfunction via paracrine signaling. In vivo, systemic Adora2b antagonism attenuated the vascular protective effects of both inosine and B420. Together, our findings support a gut microbiota-dependent component of nifedipine-mediated vascular protection that extends beyond blood pressure lowering, involving B420, increased inosine availability, and Adora2b signaling. We also nominate B420 and inosine as candidate adjuncts to calcium channel blocker therapy.

C.title: Quassin ameliorates acute cerebral infarction with attenuation of NF-κB signaling and neuroinflammation.
C.abstract: Acute cerebral infarction is a severe cerebrovascular disease characterized by neuronal injury, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammatory activation. Quassin is a bioactive quassinoid isolated from Quassia amara with reported antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities; however, its protective effects against cerebral ischemic injury and the underlying mechanisms remain to be further clarified. Cell viability was detected using the Cell Counting Kit-8 assay. Inflammatory cytokines were measured by quantitative polymerase chain reaction and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, intracellular reactive oxygen species were detected by DCFH-DA staining and flow cytometry, and nuclear factor kappa B pathway activation was analyzed by immunohistochemistry and Western blotting. Moreover, quassin reduced reactive oxygen species accumulation and decreased the expression of interleukin-1 beta, interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor alpha, and inducible nitric oxide synthase. At the molecular level, quassin reduced the phosphorylation of IκBα and p65, consistent with attenuated NF-κB signaling activation. The nuclear factor kappa B inhibitor pyrrolidine dithiocarbamate further supported the involvement of this pathway. These findings suggest that the protective effects of quassin against cerebral ischemic injury are associated with reduced oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and NF-κB signaling activation.

This study explores the mechanism of A20, A26, and co-crystal-designed compound targeting non-competitive allosteric PTP1B enzyme inhibition for AD therapy using network pharmacology and computational studies. Protein-protein interaction was designed for 128 active targets by STRING database and Cytoscape software. Further, active target-associated pathways analysed using ClueGO plugin Cytoscape software and the Reactome online public domain server. The non-competitive allosteric PTP1B inhibition through the design of Simufilam derivatives, with particular emphasis on A20, which is predicted to bind at the non-competitive allosteric site of the PTP1B protein (PDB ID: 1T49), involves α3, α6, and α7 helices that influence the WPD loop orientation. The proposed non-competitive allosteric binding mode is based on computational evidence and for that further experimental validation would be required to conclusively confirm binding of the designed compounds within this regulatory region. Using in-silico approaches, including molecular docking, identified A20 with the most favourable predicted binding energy score (-10.8 kcal/mol) compared to other derivatives. Molecular dynamics simulations further indicated structural stability of the PTP1B-A20, 26, and co-crystal complex, with consistent RMSD, RMSF, H-bond, Rg, and SASA. Principal component analysis suggested that A20 restricts conformational flexibility; hence MM-PBSA analysis displayed its stable binding free energies. Density functional theory (DFT) calculation characterized the polarity, stability, and reactivity of A20 studies supported its favourable electronic configuration. Overall, A20 displayed superior calculated binding energies, trajectory stability, and predicted drug-likeness, positioning it as a promising lead candidate for future empirical validation in AD research.

C.title: Establishment of Rat Endometriosis Model by Autologous Endometrial Transplantation and Proof-of-Concept Pharmacological Validation with Elagolix.
C.abstract: Endometriosis (EM) is a common chronic gynecological disorder in women of reproductive age, yet its pathogenesis remains unclear, and current therapeutic options are limited by significant side effects. Endometriosis itself increases the risk of premature ovarian failure. Long-term lack of standardized treatment may accelerate the decline of ovarian function and prematurely trigger the aging process of the reproductive system. Reliable animal models are therefore essential for investigating disease mechanisms and evaluating novel treatments. This study presents a detailed protocol for establishing an endometriosis model in Sprague‑Dawley (SD) rats via autologous endometrial transplantation, and evaluates the therapeutic efficacy of the FDA‑approved gonadotropin‑releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonist Elagolix. The method involved excising uterine tissue, isolating endometrial fragments, and suturing them onto the peritoneal wall. At 21 days post‑surgery, ectopic lesions with typical cystic morphology had successfully formed in 18 out of 20 rats (90% success rate). Following model validation, Elagolix administration (100 mg/kg daily, oral gavage for 4 weeks) significantly reduced final lesion volume compared with the model group (inhibition rate: 86.7%), decreased serum levels of follicle‑stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), and estradiol (E2), and suppressed peritoneal cytokine levels, including tumor necrosis factor‑α (TNF‑α), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and interleukin‑6 (IL‑6). Histopathological examination revealed glandular atrophy, reduced epithelial proliferation, and diminished inflammatory infiltration in Elagolix‑treated lesions. The model demonstrated several advantages, including operational simplicity, high stability, and avoidance of immune rejection. The pharmacological response to GnRH antagonism in this model demonstrated biological activity consistent with the known mechanism of Elagolix, although pain-related and behavioral outcomes were not evaluated. Collectively, this model provides a standardized and reliable platform for mechanistic studies and preclinical drug efficacy assessment in endometriosis.

C.title: Echinacea and Ginger combination reduces inflammatory responses of preeclamptic placental cells.
C.abstract: Preeclampsia (PE) is a severe pregnancy-related condition characterized by high blood pressure and, in some cases, proteinuria and multiorgan dysfunction, with high risk of mother and newborn mortality. Women affected by PE often experience an exacerbated inflammatory response, with elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines detected both systemically and locally in the placenta. Echinacea angustifolia and Zingiber officinale are natural compounds with well-documented anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties. Due to their minimal adverse effects for mother and fetus, they are often used during pregnancy; however, limited information is available regarding their impact on placental cells. An in vitro approach was employed using qPCR and whole-cell ELISA to study the anti-inflammatory effects of the combination of Echinacea and Ginger (ECHI + GIN) on endothelial cell lines (HUVECs) and a monocytic cell line (THP-1). The findings were further validated in primary endothelial cells isolated from preeclamptic decidual tissues (DECs-PE). We did not observe a synergistic effect between the two compounds, particularly in endothelial cells. While these compounds influenced THP-1, these effects were markedly attenuated by the cultivation in gravid serum. ECHI + GIN treatment downregulated the chronic inflammatory response, acting on the expression of CCL2/MCP-1 and VCAM1, which are involved in macrophage recruitment.

C.title: Flow-induced, inflammation-mediated arterial wall remodeling in the formation and progression of intracranial aneurysms.
C.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Unruptured intracranial aneurysms (UIAs) are relatively common lesions that may cause devastating intracranial hemorrhage, thus producing considerable suffering and anxiety in those affected by the disease or an increased likelihood of developing it. Advances in the knowledge of the pathobiology behind intracranial aneurysm (IA) formation, progression, and rupture have led to preclinical testing of drug therapies that would prevent IA formation or progression. In parallel, novel biologically based diagnostic tools to estimate rupture risk are approaching clinical use. Arterial wall remodeling, triggered by flow and intramural stresses and mediated by inflammation, is relevant to both.
METHODS: This review discusses the basis of flow-driven vessel remodeling and translates that knowledge to the observations made on the mechanisms of IA initiation and progression on studies using animal models of induced IA formation, study of human IA tissue samples, and study of patient-derived computational fluid dynamics models.
RESULTS: Blood flow conditions leading to high wall shear stress (WSS) activate proinflammatory signaling in endothelial cells that recruits macrophages to the site exposed to high WSS, especially through macrophage chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP1). This macrophage infiltration leads to protease expression, which disrupts the internal elastic lamina and collagen matrix, leading to focal outward bulging of the wall and IA initiation. For the IA to grow, collagen remodeling and smooth muscle cell (SMC) proliferation are essential, because the fact that collagen does not distend much prevents the passive dilation of a focal weakness to a sizable IA. Chronic macrophage infiltration of the IA wall promotes this SMC-mediated growth and is a potential target for drug therapy. Once the IA wall grows, it is subjected to changes in wall tension and flow conditions as a result of the change in geometry and has to remodel accordingly to avoid rupture. Flow affects this remodeling process.
CONCLUSIONS: Flow triggers an inflammatory reaction that predisposes the arterial wall to IA initiation and growth and affects the associated remodeling of the UIA wall. This chronic inflammation is a putative target for drug therapy that would stabilize UIAs or prevent UIA formation. Moreover, once this coupling between IA wall remodeling and flow is understood, data from patient-specific flow models can be gathered as part of the diagnostic workup and utilized to improve risk assessment for UIA initiation, progression, and eventual rupture.

C.title: Glioblastoma immune landscape remodeling following treatment with CD70-targeted CAR-T cells.
C.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has shown limited efficacy in glioblastoma (GB), largely because of the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We have previously demonstrated that the ligand-based mCD70-directed construct mCAR27 specifically eliminates CD70⁺ GB cells in vitro, and induces durable tumor remission with prolonged survival in a syngeneic model of orthotopic GB. Despite the therapeutic promise of CD70 as a GB CAR-T cell target, the impact of CD70-directed CAR-T cells on the brain tumor immune landscape after target interception remains unexplored. Here, we independently confirmed a tumorigenic role for CD70 in murine GB by performing bulk RNA sequencing and in vivo experiments. Next, we applied single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) to decipher the transcriptome of GB-infiltrating immune cells in immunocompetent mice bearing CD70+ GB after intratumoral mCAR27 therapy. CAR-T cell treatment expanded adoptively transferred cells and was associated with increased endogenous Cd8⁺ T-cell infiltration, alongside a reduction in immunosuppressive populations, including Tregs and anti-inflammatory M2-like macrophages, but also subsets of dendritic and natural-killer cells. CD70 expression was detected on multiple GB-infiltrating immune subsets, notably Tregs and M2-like macrophages. Transcriptionally, mCAR27-mediated GB remission led to a coordinated downregulation of type-I interferon-stimulated genes and immunosuppressive mediators such as Arg1, Tgfbi, Cd274, Pdcd1lg2 and Lag3, coupled with upregulation of genes involved in inflammatory resolution, findings consistent with attenuation of GB-derived inflammatory stress and immunosuppression. Collectively, we showcase that CD70-directed CAR-T cell therapy remodels the post-treatment immune landscape towards resolution of inflammation and reduced immunosuppression, supporting sustained immune surveillance.

C.title: Efficacy and safety of tolebrutinib in multiple sclerosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
C.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tolebrutinib is an oral, brain-penetrant Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor being investigated for multiple sclerosis (MS). Early data point to reduced relapse rates and radiological disease activity, along with a reassuring safety profile. This systematic review and meta-analysis bring together the available evidence on its clinical efficacy and adverse events.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus through February 2026 using predefined eligibility criteria. Data were extracted on efficacy outcomes (disability progression and improvement, MRI activity, and brain volume change) and safety outcomes (any adverse events, serious adverse events, adverse events leading to discontinuation, headache, ALT elevation, and death). Continuous outcomes were pooled as means using reported means and standard deviations; proportional outcomes were pooled from event and total counts. Analyses were run in R using random-effects models, with data unsuitable for pooling described narratively.
RESULTS: Four publications met our inclusion criteria: three reporting four randomized controlled trials and one long-term extension study. Tolebrutinib reduced the risk of confirmed disability progression at both ≥3 and ≥6 months, and disability improvement at 6 months was numerically higher than with comparators, though not conclusively so. Pooled progression rates were 18.35% (95% CI 9.73-31.9) at ≥3 months and 14.08% (95% CI 6.78-26.95) at ≥6 months. Mean brain volume change was -0.69% (95% CI -0.73 to -0.65). Adverse events of any kind occurred in 75.98% of patients, serious adverse events in 11.26%, and discontinuation due to adverse events in 4.14%; deaths were rare.
CONCLUSION: The available trial evidence suggests that tolebrutinib may reduce confirmed disability progression in nonrelapsing secondary progressive MS and MRI inflammatory activity versus placebo in earlier-phase relapsing MS. These findings are preliminary and should not be interpreted as definitive comparative evidence; longer-term, adequately powered studies are needed to define durability, safety, and its place relative to established disease-modifying therapies.

C.title: Aerobic exercise ameliorates cardiac function in HFpEF mice by suppressing ALCAT1, neuroinflammation and oxidative stress in the paraventricular nucleus and nucleus tractus solitarius.
C.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is commonly accompanied by sympathetic overactivation, contributing to poor patient prognosis. The paraventricular nucleus (PVN) and nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) are critical cardiovascular regulatory centers. Pathological cardiolipin (CL) remodeling catalyzed by Acyl-CoA:lysocardiolipin acyltransferase 1 (ALCAT1) exacerbates disease progression. This study aims to elucidate the roles of aerobic exercise and ALCAT1 in modulating brain-heart axis dysregulation in HFpEF.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We employed wild-type (WT) and Alcat1 knockout mice to establish an HFpEF model, followed by aerobic exercise. Neuroinflammatory model was established to investigate the role of ALCAT1 in neuroinflammation. Underlying mechanisms were explored in HT22 cells. In HFpEF mice, aerobic exercise suppressed ALCAT1 and up-regulated growth differentiation factor 5 (GDF5) in the PVN and NTS, reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines, enhanced antioxidant enzyme activities, decreased oxidative stress markers, and attenuated neuronal structural damage and hyperactivation. These central improvements were accompanied by attenuated cardiac sympathetic overactivation, lowered blood pressure, and improved diastolic function. The important role of ALCAT1 was further supported, as its genetic knockout conferred significant protection in both HFpEF and neuroinflammatory models. In HT22 cells, GDF5 suppressed the LPS-induced ALCAT1 up-regulation and ameliorated cellular injury.
CONCLUSION: ALCAT1 is an important contributor to neuronal injury. Aerobic exercise suppresses ALCAT1 and up-regulates GDF5, ameliorating neuronal injury and improving diastolic function in HFpEF mice. Mechanistically, ALCAT1 and GDF5 are reciprocally regulated, which may contribute to the protective effects of aerobic exercise against HFpEF. These findings suggest ALCAT1 as a potential molecular target for exercise-based HFpEF therapy.

C.title: Tumor endothelial cells as vascular immune gatekeepers: reprogramming the vascular-immune interface for cancer immunotherapy.
C.abstract: Despite durable clinical responses to immunotherapy in a subset of patients, most solid tumors remain refractory owing to an immune-excluded phenotype characterized by limited trafficking, infiltration, and function of effector immune cells within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Tumor endothelial cells (TECs) function as vascular immune gatekeepers that orchestrate this process. Driven by persistent pro-angiogenic signaling and metabolic stress, TECs establish a multilayered immune barrier through structurally abnormal, poorly perfused vasculature, endothelial anergy, and active immunosuppressive programs. TECs directly suppress effector T-cell and natural killer (NK)-cell function through checkpoint-like ligands, death-ligand pathways, and immunometabolic mechanisms involving adenosine production and tryptophan catabolism. Simultaneously, they recruit, retain, and reprogram immunosuppressive leukocytes, thereby reinforcing immune exclusion and therapeutic resistance. Here, we propose a TEC-centric vascular immune gatekeeping framework and review strategies to reprogram tumor vessels from immune barriers into conduits for effective immune-cell trafficking and activation. We discuss endothelial-directed monotherapies that transiently normalize or reset TEC states, together with combination strategies integrating vascular modulation with immune checkpoint blockade, adoptive and innate immune-cell therapies, cancer vaccines, oncolytic viruses, STING agonists, and multifunctional antibodies. We also highlight key translational considerations, including biomarker-guided patient stratification, pharmacodynamic monitoring using mechanism-based endpoints, and optimization of treatment dose and scheduling within the vascular normalization window. Overall, this review establishes endothelial reprogramming as a central strategy for overcoming vascular immune gatekeeping and provides a mechanistic framework for biomarker-guided vascular-immune combination therapies in solid tumors.

C.title: Metabolic Competition-Driven Antitumor Immunity of glpX-Deficient Engineered Salmonella via Glucose Deprivation and STING Activation in Bladder Cancer.
C.abstract: Background: Bacteria-mediated cancer therapy is emerging as a promising approach due to its low cost, scalability, and sustained efficacy. While bacterial immunomodulation has been extensively studied, the role of bacterial metabolic competition, particularly for glucose, in tumor suppression remains unclear. We aimed to investigate how engineered Salmonella strains exploit metabolic competition to trigger antitumor immunity and improve therapeutic outcomes in bladder cancer models. Methods: Using genetic screening, we generated a gluconeogenesis-deficient Salmonella strain, the AISIH strain with the glpX gene knocked out (GLA1), with enhanced glucose uptake. In vitro and in vivo assays were performed to assess tumor cell glucose deprivation, mitochondrial stress, cytosolic mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release, and activation of the cGAS/STING pathway. An engineered strain, GLA2, was generated from the AISIH strain by knockout of the glpX gene and was subsequently further engineered to locally deliver an anti-tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) nanobody under quorum-sensing control. Efficacy was evaluated in subcutaneous and orthotopic bladder cancer models, with analysis of tumor-infiltrating immune cells, dendritic cell (DC) maturation, and T cell priming. Results: GLA1 competitively depleted glucose in the bladder tumor microenvironment, inducing energy stress, mitochondrial damage, and mtDNA release, which noncanonically activated the STING pathway. This promoted type I interferon production, DC maturation, and antitumor immune responses. However, TNF-α-mediated vascular abnormalities limited efficacy. GLA2 normalized tumor vasculature via local anti-TNF-α delivery, enhancing nutrient competition and immune activation. Both strains markedly suppressed tumor growth, with GLA2 showing superior efficacy due to synergistic metabolic and immune reprogramming. Conclusions: This study demonstrates that bacterial competition for glucose is a pivotal mechanism of antitumor activity in bladder cancer, linking metabolic stress to STING-dependent immune activation. Engineered Salmonella strains that combine enhanced glucose uptake with local vascular normalization offer a robust platform for bladder cancer. These findings highlight a novel strategy to integrate microbial metabolic engineering with immune modulation, providing a foundation for precision bacteriotherapy in oncology.

C.title: Omega-3 Fatty Acid Pretreatment Modulates Mitochondrial Quality-Control and PINK1/PARKIN-Related Gene Expression in Acute LPS-Induced Neuroinflammation.
C.abstract: Neuroinflammation contributes to central nervous system injury through interconnected oxidative, glial, apoptotic, and mitochondrial responses. Omega-3 (OM-3) fatty acids are neuroprotective, but their association with mitochondrial quality-control pathways during acute neuroinflammation remains incompletely defined. This study examined the preventive effects of OM-3 pretreatment in a lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced neuroinflammation model. Adult female Wistar albino rats (n = 8/group) were randomly assigned to Control, LPS (5 mg/kg, intraperitoneal), LPS + OM-3 (OM-3, 0.5 g/kg/day intraperitoneally for 3 days before LPS), and OM-3 groups. Six hours after LPS administration, brain and cerebellar tissues were evaluated by histopathology, immunohistochemistry (8-OHdG, Cas-3, and GFAP), qRT-PCR for apoptosis-, antioxidant-, mitochondrial biogenesis-, and mitophagy-related transcripts, and biochemical assessment of total antioxidant status (TAS), total oxidant status (TOS), and oxidative stress index (OSI). LPS increased histopathological injury and 8-OHdG, Cas-3, and GFAP immunoreactivity; increased BAX/BCL-2, PINK1, PARKIN, and SNCA transcript levels; reduced PGC-1alpha and NRF2-related antioxidant responses; decreased TAS; and increased OSI. OM-3 pretreatment attenuated many of these changes relative to LPS alone. However, several outcomes remained significantly different from Control, indicating partial rather than complete reversal. Because PINK1 and PARKIN were measured only at the mRNA level, the findings demonstrate modulation of the transcriptional response of mitophagy-related genes and do not establish functional mitophagic flux. In this 6-h acute preventive model, OM-3 pretreatment was associated with partial neuroprotection and modulation of transcriptional markers linked to antioxidant defense and mitochondrial quality Control. Protein-level and flux assays, later time points, and post-injury treatment designs are required before functional restoration of mitophagy or therapeutic efficacy can be concluded.

C.title: Network pharmacology-based investigation on the mechanism of aloin in ameliorating atherosclerosis by regulating macrophage polarization.
C.abstract: Atherosclerosis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory vascular disease in which macrophage polarization plays a pivotal role in plaque progression and stability. Aloin, a major anthraquinone compound isolated from Aloe vera, possesses potent anti-inflammatory activities; however, its therapeutic potential and underlying mechanisms in AS remain insufficiently understood. In the present study, a network pharmacology approach combined with molecular docking, cellular experiments, and animal validation was employed to investigate the protective effects of aloin against AS and elucidate its molecular mechanism. Common targets shared by aloin, macrophage polarization, and AS were identified, followed by protein-protein interaction network construction and GO/KEGG enrichment analyses. Molecular docking demonstrated strong binding affinities of aloin toward key inflammatory targets, particularly NF-κB and STAT3. Experimental validation showed that aloin significantly suppressed nitric oxide production in lipopolysaccharide-induced RAW264.7 macrophages and inhibited M1 macrophage polarization while promoting the M2 phenotype, as evidenced by decreased expression of iNOS and TNF-α and increased expression of Arg-1 and IL-10. In ApoE-/- mice fed a high-fat diet, aloin markedly reduced aortic plaque formation and alleviated vascular pathological injury. Mechanistically, both in vitro and in vivo analyses revealed that aloin significantly attenuated the phosphorylation of NF-κB and STAT3, thereby blocking activation of the NF-κB/STAT3 signaling pathway. Collectively, these findings suggest that aloin may contribute to the amelioration of atherosclerotic lesions by modulating macrophage polarization balance through inhibition of NF-κB/STAT3 signaling, highlighting its potential as a candidate worthy of further investigation for the prevention and treatment of atherosclerosis.

C.title: Current practices in elective embolisation: insights from a UK national cross-sectional survey.
C.abstract:
AIM: The aim of this study was to evaluate the national landscape of elective embolisation services in the UK and identify factors affecting service delivery and expansion.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: An online cross-sectional survey comprising 19 structured questions exploring the current provision of arterial and venous elective embolisation procedures, service capacity, resource availability, and training was distributed to approximately 1,000 members of a national society in March 2025. Quantitative and qualitative analyses were performed.
RESULTS: Eighty-five responses from 54 UK National Health Service (NHS) Trusts were analysed, predominantly from consultant interventional radiologists (85%), working in tertiary centres (62%), district general hospitals (24%), or both (14%). Elective arterial and venous embolisation procedures were widely performed, most commonly uterine artery (94%), renal angiomyolipoma (92%), visceral aneurysm (89%), and varicocele (98%) embolisation. Tumour, type II endoleak, prostate artery, and arteriovenous malformation embolisation were performed significantly more frequently in tertiary centres (P < .05). Most reported access to day-case beds (87%) and clinic time (84%), although provision was frequently perceived as insufficient. While 63% expressed a desire to expand services, key barriers included funding (55%), inadequate referral pathways (45%), bed capacity (39% day-case; 37% inpatient), emergency workload (36%), and workforce shortages (36% radiologists; 36% nurses/radiographers). Qualitative feedback highlighted resource limitations, regional disparities, and the need for more flexible training pathways.
CONCLUSION: Sustainable expansion of elective embolisation across the UK requires clinically integrated interventional radiology (IR) services, protected capacity, infrastructure and workforce investment, regional networks, standardisation, flexible training, and systematic evaluation.

C.title: Localized hydrogel depots for CAR-T cell therapy in solid tumors: materials design, cellular fitness and translational deployment.
C.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy is less effective in solid tumors than in selected hematologic malignancies because vascular, stromal, spatial, and immunosuppressive barriers restrict cell delivery and function. Local hydrogels and related biomaterials can convert a transient administration into a spatially organized depot, but their benefit depends on more than polymer identity. This review therefore combines a scenario-driven framework-depot versus bolus, intratumoral versus peritumoral placement, unresected versus postsurgical disease, and cell-loaded versus cell-free support-with a materials-centered analysis of formation, administration, time-dependent mechanics, architecture, degradation, biochemical presentation, and manufacturing. Direct evidence is distinguished from adjacent mechanistic evidence and design hypotheses. Across the available studies, the best-supported functions are improved delivered-cell recovery, regional persistence, controlled presentation of supportive cues, and enhanced antitumor activity in selected preclinical models. By contrast, universal material-property optima, clinically validated hydrogel-CAR-T products, and cryopreservation of a final cell-loaded depot have not been established. We define practical tests for gelation and device compatibility, productive egression, material-to-cell fitness, component attribution, and integrated-product safety. A materials-focused comparative table and a 30-study evidence map separate measured values from inferred mechanisms and identify where CAR-T cells were directly loaded, administered separately, manufactured in a matrix, or generated in situ. The resulting framework emphasizes that successful platforms must coordinate material behavior, CAR-T quality, anatomical placement, and clinical workflow rather than maximizing retention or chemical complexity alone.

C.title: Androgen Receptor (AR) Expression is Associated with an Immune-Cold Phenotype and Reduced Response to Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors in ER-Positive/HER2-Negative Breast Cancer.
C.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have limited efficacy in estrogen receptor-positive/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative (ER+/HER2-) breast cancer, and the mechanisms underlying immune resistance remain unclear. The androgen receptor gene (AR), expressed in a substantial proportion of ER-positive tumors, has been implicated in tumor biology; however, its role in the tumor immune microenvironment and immunotherapy response is not well understood.
METHODS: We investigated the association between AR expression, transcriptome-derived immune cell-associated signatures, and response to ICIs in 4046 patients with breast cancer across five cohorts with bulk transcriptomic data and two cohorts with single-cell transcriptomic data.
RESULTS: High AR expression was consistently associated with reduced transcriptome-derived tumor-infiltrating leukocyte scores across multiple ER+/HER2- cohorts. Specifically, signatures associated with cluster of differentiation (CD)-8+ T-cell subsets, dendritic cells, and M1 macrophages were significantly reduced in AR-high tumors, indicating a transcriptionally immune-suppressed tumor microenvironment. In the I-SPY2 cohort, AR-high tumors demonstrated significantly lower pathological complete response rates after neoadjuvant ICI therapy. Furthermore, AR expression showed a predictive performance for ICI response that was superior to that with programmed cell death protein-1 and programmed cell death ligand-1 (area under the curve 0.82 vs. 0.73 and 0.60, respectively). Interestingly, single-cell analysis revealed that AR expression across multiple cell types, including epithelial, endothelial, and myeloid, was associated with reduced ICI responsiveness. Additionally, AR inhibition using enzalutamide was associated with increased signatures associated with CD8+ T cells, dendritic cells, and M1 macrophages.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that AR expression is associated with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and reduced response to ICIs in ER+/HER2- breast cancer.

C.title: Therapeutic potential analysis of Sertoli cell-derived exosomes in cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury.
C.abstract: Cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury is a core pathological process underlying further neurological deterioration after reperfusion therapy for acute ischemic stroke. Developing more effective neuroprotective agents is therefore a current priority in neuroscience research. Sertoli cells possess unique immunoprivileged and nutritional support functions within the testes and secrete exosomes that serve as important mediators of intercellular communication, with substantial potential for neuroprotection. This review addresses the protective mechanisms of Sertoli cell-derived exosomes in cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury. Through a comprehensive literature review, we systematically summarize their neuroprotective effects, including the modulation of immune and inflammatory responses, inhibition of cellular apoptosis, promotion of neurovascular repair, regulation of autophagy, and influence on epigenetic modifications and related signaling pathways. By synthesizing the latest findings in this field, we aim to provide insights into the development and translation of novel neuroprotective strategies based on Sertoli cell-derived exosomes.

C.title: Activated B cells steer fibroblasts towards a proinflammatory phenotype in giant cell arteritis.
C.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is characterized by chronic large-vessel inflammation and remodelling. Within affected arteries, especially in aorta, organized B cell clusters are mainly localized in adventitia, where fibroblasts represent the dominant stromal population. This study aims to investigate fibroblast heterogeneity within these clusters and B cell-fibroblast interactions in vitro as possible contributors to disease chronicity in GCA.
METHODS: Fibroblast phenotypes in CD20+B cell clusters in GCA and atherosclerotic aortic tissues were characterized using immunohistochemistry for fibroblast markers (CD90, PDPN, FAP, CD248, α-SMA) and cytokine expression (IL-6, GM-CSF, BAFF). In vitro, peripheral blood B cells from treatment-naïve GCA patients and healthy donors were stimulated and cocultured with human aortic adventitial fibroblasts (HAoAFs) using either direct cell coculture or transwell systems. To identify relevant molecular pathways for B cell-fibroblast interaction, HAoAFs were pre-treated with infliximab, tocilizumab, baricitinib or upadacitinib, followed by exposure to activated B cell conditioned medium (aBCCM). Protein secretion was assessed by ELISA, Luminex and Olink, mRNA expression was determined by qPCR.
RESULTS: CD90+PDPN+immunofibroblasts mainly localized centrally, whereas CD90+FAP+ and CD90+CD248+fibroblasts mostly located at the border of the clusters. Fibroblasts in/around clusters co-expressed IL-6, GM-CSF, and BAFF. In vitro, HAoAFs cocultured with activated B cells or supernatants thereof upregulated IL-6, GM-CSF, PDPN, and FAP mRNA, and actively secreted IL-6, GM-CSF and BAFF, while type I collagen expression was suppressed. JAK-STAT inhibition abrogated these pro-inflammatory effects, whereas TNF-α and IL-6 receptor blockade did not.
CONCLUSION: Activated B cells drive fibroblasts toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype, potentially sustaining chronic inflammation and disease progression in GCA. JAK-STAT signalling appears central to this effect, highlighting its therapeutic potency at the vascular level in GCA.

C.title: Spatial polarization of endothelial ICAM-1 governs T-cell exclusion in melanoma.
C.abstract: An immunosuppressive microenvironment limits therapeutic efficacy in melanoma. Beyond T-cell abundance and function, tumor control depends on T-cell access to malignant cells, yet the vascular mechanisms governing T-cell positioning remain poorly defined. Using RNA sequencing of endothelial cells from tumor cores versus peripheries in a mouse melanoma model, we identified intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) as a candidate regulator of T-cell localization. During tumor growth, T cells shifted from a balanced core-margin distribution to marked exclusion from the core, particularly in T cell-inflamed tumors. This spatial polarization, less evident in other immune subsets, coincided with high expression of lymphocyte function-associated antigen-1 (LFA-1) on T cells. Endothelial ICAM-1 became enriched at the tumor periphery, where vascular integrity was compromised, with increased vascular leakage and reduced pericyte coverage. ICAM-1 blockade restored T-cell infiltration, enhanced effector activity, and delayed growth of immunogenic tumors, and sensitized an immune-refractory tumor to anti-PD-1 blockade. These findings identify endothelial ICAM-1 as a vascular determinant of T-cell positioning and the ICAM-1/LFA-1 axis as a modifiable checkpoint to enhance antitumor immunity and immunotherapy efficacy.

C.title: Surgical management of Rasmussen's encephalitis: A systematic review and meta-analysis of long-term seizure and functional outcomes.
C.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Rasmussen's encephalitis (RE) is a rare, progressive inflammatory brain disease often leading to drug-resistant epilepsy and severe neurological decline. While surgery is the definitive treatment, evidence remains fragmented due to the rarity of the condition. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy of various surgical techniques and identify predictors of long-term seizure freedom.
METHODS: We performed a comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. We included studies reporting surgical outcomes in patients with RE. Pooled proportions were calculated using random-effects meta-analysis, and meta-regression was employed to investigate predictors of seizure freedom, including age at surgery and surgical technique.
RESULTS: Thirty-one studies comprising 460 patients were included. The overall pooled rate of long-term seizure freedom (Engel Class I/ILAE Class 1) was 65.0% (95% CI: 53.0%-76.0%). Subgroup pooling demonstrated high rates of long-term seizure freedom following complete hemispheric disconnection procedures, with hemispherotomy achieving 75.0% (95% CI: 63.0%-85.0%) and functional hemispherectomy achieving 66.0% (95% CI: 50.0%-80.0%). However, meta-regression confirmed no statistically significant difference in efficacy between disconnective techniques (p = 0.2243). In contrast, focal or less-than-hemispheric resections demonstrated significantly inferior efficacy (35.0%, p = 0.0086). Meta-regression analysis indicated that earlier age at surgery was a robust predictor of superior long-term seizure outcomes (beta = -0.0383, p = 0.0165), explaining 27.98% of between-study heterogeneity. Shorter disease duration prior to surgery was likewise significantly associated with higher seizure freedom (beta = -0.0412, p = 0.0210). A modest trend toward improved outcomes was observed in recent publication eras. Baseline clinical severity (preoperative EPC, hemiparesis) and complication rates were not significant predictors. Postoperative gross motor function and language preservation were generally stable, ranging from 67.7% to 94.1% and 84-93.1%, respectively.
CONCLUSION: Complete hemispheric disconnection (whether via hemispherotomy or functional hemispherectomy) is highly effective for controlling seizures in RE, whereas focal resections provide inadequate control. Earlier surgical intervention and shorter disease duration significantly improve long-term seizure freedom. These findings support prompt referral for hemispheric disconnection in patients with medically refractory RE rather than delaying surgery with prolonged immunomodulatory trials.

C.title: AAV-mediated Siglecf elimination on TAMs reverses TMZ therapy-induced T cell dysfunction in glioblastoma.
C.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive primary tumor of the brain, characterized by extensive intratumor heterogeneity, and exhibits inevitable recurrence despite conventional therapy. This study investigates the immunosuppressive mechanisms underlying GBM recurrence following temozolomide (TMZ) therapy, with a specific focus on macrophage-associated pathways driving immune evasion. By integrating single-cell RNA sequencing and mass cytometry time-of-flight analyses in orthotopic mouse GBM models, we revealed extensive transcriptional and phenotypic remodeling of the tumor microenvironment after TMZ treatment, including reduced malignant cell proliferation, activation of cytokine-mediated signaling, pronounced T-cell exhaustion, and a shift of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) toward immunosuppressive sialic acid-binding Ig-like lectin F (Siglec-F, encoded by Siglecf) positive subsets. Functional validation demonstrated that expression of Siglec-F inhibited macrophage phagocytosis and enhanced immunosuppression, whereas Siglecf-targeted intervention using adeno-associated virus (AAV) restored T-cell activation and improved antitumor efficacy. Analyses of human GBM datasets confirmed the enrichment of SIGLEC5+ (human homolog of murine Siglecf) TAMs in recurrent tumors, correlating with adverse prognosis. Collectively, our findings suggest a TMZ-induced immunosuppressive reprogramming of GBM microenvironment and implicate Siglec-F/SIGLEC5+ TAMs as potential mediators of immune escape and promising therapeutic targets to overcome chemoresistance.

C.title: Microglia and border-associated macrophages play opposite roles in cerebrovascular and leukocyte responses under systemic inflammation in male mice.
C.abstract: Microglia closely associate with the vasculature, but their roles in leukocyte trafficking and cerebral blood flow (CBF) during systemic inflammation are unclear. We show that sustained systemic inflammation leads to altered microglia-vascular interactions, leukocyte recruitment to cerebral blood vessels and reduced hypercapnia-induced vasodilation. We find that microglia and border-associated macrophages (BAMs) play distinct roles in these processes: while BAM depletion with clodronate increases leukocyte recruitment, microglia/BAM depletion with PLX5622 and the absence of microglia, but not BAMs in CSF1RΔFIRE/ΔFIRE mice, result in markedly reduced leukocyte recruitment. Supporting this, conditional microglial IL-1 deletion inhibits leukocyte recruitment. Unlike BAM depletion, the absence of microglia impairs hypercapnia-induced vasodilation, while in vivo two-photon imaging reveals microglial IL-1α-dependent interactions between leukocytes and penetrating arteries. Accordingly, reduced hypercapnia-induced vasodilation involves endothelial IL-1R1 and microglial IL-1α. Thus, distinct brain macrophage populations exert opposite effects on leukocyte recruitment and CBF through IL-1 dependent mechanisms in given vascular beds in male mice.

C.title: microRNAs in Cerebrovascular Disease.
C.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases are major causes of morbidity and mortality in developed countries. Cerebrovascular diseases, especially stroke, represent major burden of disability and economy impact. Major advances in primary and secondary prevention and therapy are needed in order to tackle this public health problem. Our better understanding of pathophysiology is essential in order to develop novel diagnostic and therapeutic tools and strategies. microRNAs are a family of important post-transcriptional regulators of gene expression and their involvement in the pathophysiology of cerebrovascular diseases has already been reported. Moreover, microRNAs may represent above-mentioned potential diagnostic and therapeutic tools in clinical practice. Within this chapter, we briefly describe basic epidemiology, aetiology and clinical manifestation of following cerebrovascular diseases: extracranial carotid atherosclerosis, acute stroke, intracranial aneurysms and cerebral arterio-venous malformations. Further, in each chapter, the current knowledge about the involvement of specific microRNAs and their potential use in clinical practice will be summarized. More specifically, within the subchapter "miRNAs in carotid atherosclerosis", general information about miRNA involvement in atherosclerosis will be described (miR-126, miR-17-92, miR-155 and others) with special emphasis put on miRNAs affecting carotid plaque progression and stability (e.g. miR-145, miR-146 or miR-217). In the subchapter "miRNAs in acute stroke", we will provide insight into recent knowledge from animal and human studies concerning miRNA profiling in acute stroke and their expression dynamics in brain tissue and extracellular fluids (roles of, e.g. let-7 family, miR-21, miR-29 family, miR-124, miR-145, miR-181 family, miR-210 and miR-223). Subchapters dealing with "miRNAs and AV malformations" and "miRNAs and intracranial aneurysms" will focus on miR-21, miR-26, miR-29 family and miR-143/145.

C.title: Imaging of vascular lesions of the head and neck.
C.abstract: The diagnosis of vascular lesions of the head and neck should be directed by classifying the lesions as tumors or malformations and by determining their flow characteristics. Location of the lesion is key when differentiating between vascular neoplasms. Ultrasonography is an appropriate screening tool; MRI is often used to confirm the diagnosis. Computed tomography can be used for further characterization of the lesion, particularly when there is bony involvement. In many cases, vascular lesions grow to be extensive. In these cases, percutaneous sclerotherapy or embolization therapy can be employed to aid in surgical resection.

C.title: Macrocephaly-capillary malformation syndrome: description of a case and review of clinical diagnostic criteria.
C.abstract: Macrocephaly-capillary malformation (M-CM) is characterized by prenatal overgrowth, variable somatic and cerebral asymmetry, primary megalencephaly, characteristic facial features, an abnormal neurocognitive profile and cutaneous vascular malformations. It was previously known under the name macrocephaly-cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenital (M-CMTC). However a recent review of the previously reported cases has suggested that the vascular anomalies are not true CMTC but rather capillary malformations. The diagnosis is primary clinical and different criteria have been proposed for this purpose. However, M-CM is frequently associated with structural brain abnormalities that should be properly investigated and monitored because of their possible progressive development. We report the neuroradiological and morphological features observed in a girl with M-CM and we compared them with proposed diagnostic criteria found in the literature.

C.title: Targeting the Calcium-mtDNA-cGAS-STING Signaling Nexus: A Novel Redox Mechanism for Nimodipine's Neuroprotection in Traumatic Brain Injury.
C.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) induces severe secondary injury where molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigates the involvement of the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) signaling pathway in this process and evaluates the neuroprotective effect of the L-type calcium channel blocker nimodipine, focusing on calcium homeostasis, mitochondrial function, and inflammatory signaling.
METHODS: Using primary neuronal and mouse TBI models, we assessed outcomes via fluorescent calcium imaging, JC-1 staining, Western blot, quantitative PCR (qPCR)/reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, and behavioral tests. Nimodipine was applied to inhibit L-type channels, specifically testing its role in reducing mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release, blocking cGAS-STING activation, and suppressing neuroinflammation.
RESULTS: TBI markedly activated the cGAS-STING pathway, increasing pro-inflammatory factors and apoptosis. In the cellular oxygen-glucose deprivation model, calcium overload was directly observed by Fluo-4 AM staining and was associated with subsequent mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening and mtDNA release, identifying this process as a key upstream event for cGAS-STING activation. Nimodipine inhibited intracellular calcium overload, reduced mitochondrial injury and mtDNA release, and consequently suppressed cGAS-STING pathway activation. Both in vivo and in vitro experiments showed dose-dependent decreases in pro-inflammatory factors, along with improved neurological function and attenuated brain tissue pathology.
CONCLUSION: Nimodipine attenuates secondary neuroinflammation and neuronal apoptosis after TBI by inhibiting calcium influx, decreasing mtDNA release, and suppressing cGAS-STING signaling. These results suggest that the Ca2+-mtDNA-cGAS-STING axis contributes to TBI pathology and that nimodipine may serve as a potential multitarget therapy. Antioxid. Redox Signal. 00, 000-000.

C.title: Stroke-associated pneumonia: from immunodepression to bedside management and future research directions.
C.abstract: Stroke-associated pneumonia (SAP) is one of the most frequent complications after acute stroke, affecting approximately one in eight stroke patients. Besides prolonged hospitalisation and increased healthcare costs, it is also a major risk factor for mortality and poor functional recovery. The pathophysiology of SAP is driven by two converging processes: impaired local airway defence due to dysphagia as well as reduced airway clearance reflexes, and systemic stroke-induced immunodepression driven by dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system. While post-stroke immunodepression is a major risk factor for SAP, it might limit unwanted autoimmune responses within the brain. Conversely, SAP itself may drive neuroinflammation and contribute to post-stroke cognitive impairment. Despite its clinical importance, high-quality evidence to guide practice on prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of SAP remains scarce and guideline recommendations are mostly based on expert consensus. Diagnosis of SAP is suggested to be based on standardised clinical criteria supported by chest radiography and C-reactive protein as an adjunct where uncertainty persists. After diagnosis, guidelines suggest prompt empirical antibiotic therapy according to local protocols. In contrast, preventive antibiotics, even for high-risk patients, neither improve clinical outcome nor reduce SAP frequency. Currently recommended preventive strategies for SAP therefore mostly focus on dysphagia management and early mobilisation. This review integrates the pathophysiology, long-term consequences of SAP and further research directions based on the current knowledge on post-stroke immunology with prevention, diagnosis and treatment of SAP as set out in the recent European Stroke Organisation guideline and related guidelines.

C.title: Postbiotics Unveiled: The Next Emerging Trend in Functional Foods.
C.abstract: The global population is expected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050, with demand for food increasing by up to 56%. Postbiotics are a safe and reliable substitute for probiotics, which are described as preparations of non-viable bacteria and/or their metabolic byproducts. Data for this narrative review was collected using Goggle scholar and PubMed from 2006 to 2026. Major bioactive compounds such as short-chain fatty acids, peptides, polysaccharides, vitamins, and cell fragments contribute to immunomodulatory, antioxidant, metabolic, and gut-brain axis effects. Preclinical and clinical research shows that they can improve insulin sensitivity, control cytokine signaling, strengthen epithelial barrier integrity, and protect against obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and depression. Postbiotics have also been found to improve mineral absorption and folate synthesis, and possess anti-sarcopenic actions. Several commercial products are available because of their health benefits. Thus, postbiotics are a revolutionary development in microbiome-based treatments; however, to completely understand their therapeutic potential, it is necessary to standardize, achieve mechanistic clarity, and ensure regulatory alignment.

C.title: Low-dose radiotherapy ameliorates Alzheimer's-like pathology in 5xFAD mice and is associated with HIF-1α-related inflammatory signaling downregulation.
C.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Whether fractionated low-dose radiotherapy (LDRT) alleviates Alzheimer's disease-like pathology and whether these effects are associated with microglial HIF-1α-related signaling remain unclear.
METHODS: Male 5xFAD mice received whole-brain irradiation at 2 Gy per fraction for 5 fractions (total dose, 10 Gy). One month later, cognition was assessed by the Morris water maze and novel object recognition tests, and brain pathology was evaluated by immunofluorescence and Western blot. LPS-stimulated BV2 cells were used as an in vitro model to examine the effects of LDRT on nitric oxide, cytokines, and reactive oxygen species. Transcriptomic analysis was performed with 3 biological replicates per group, followed by pharmacological validation using the HIF-1α inhibitor YC-1.
RESULTS: LDRT improved spatial and recognition memory, reduced Aβ plaque burden in the hippocampus and cortex, and attenuated microglial activation in 5xFAD mice. In particular, LDRT decreased the hippocampal Aβ plaque area fraction (P = 0.0065) and reduced HIF-1α expression in Iba1-positive microglia in the hippocampus (P = 0.0077). In addition, LDRT reduced Iba1 expression and CD68-positive area while preserving Aβ phagocytosis by primary microglia. In BV2 cells, LDRT inhibited LPS-induced inflammatory responses and altered 123 differentially expressed genes enriched in the HIF-1, IL-17, TNF, MAPK, and p53 signaling pathways. Pharmacological inhibition of HIF-1α by YC-1 recapitulated, but did not further enhance, the anti-inflammatory effects of LDRT.
CONCLUSIONS: Fractionated whole-brain LDRT ameliorates cognitive deficits and Aβ pathology in 5xFAD mice, with effects associated with downregulation of microglial HIF-1α-related signaling.

C.title: IRE-1α/XBP-1s axis determines phosphodiesterase 1c activation inducing vascular endothelial cell damage, contributes to cerebral vascular injury and neuroinflammation.
C.abstract: Cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase 1 (PDE1) plays critical roles in mediating neuroinflammation, neuron degeneration, and cognitive impairment through suppressing the fundamental cAMP and cGMP signaling, presenting a promising therapeutic target in combating neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative disease. However, the crucial mechanism correlating PDE1 activation and how it regulates neuroinflammation are less studied. Here, we found that the level of PDE1c significantly increased in the cerebral tissue of cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) rats, especially of the endothelial cell population. Treating the human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC) with oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R) or dithiothreitol (DTT) significantly increased the expression level of PDE1c at both transcription and translation levels and induced vascular cell damage. These were alongside IRE-1α/XBP-1s axis activation. Inhibition of IRE-1α/XBP-1s axis by pharmacological interventions such as TUDCA or PAIR2 or gene silencing efficiently decreased PDE1c level and ameliorated vascular cell damage. Moreover, deficiency or inhibition of PDE1c by its inhibitor PDE1-IN-4 suppressed vascular cell damage and inflammatory markers activation but marginally affected IRE-1α/XBP-1s axis. Also, no additive effects were observed when treating PDE1-IN-4 in the Xbp-1s knockdown cells. Collectively, our study revealed that IRE-1α/XBP-1s axis might be a crucial upstream regulator of PDE1c in controlling vascular endothelial barrier homeostasis, presenting a novel therapeutic strategy in ameliorating CIRI.

C.title: Selective CB2 receptor activation attenuates neuroinflammation and preserves immune responsiveness after photothrombotic stroke.
C.abstract: Ischemic stroke triggers neuroinflammation that can drive CNS injury-induced immunodepression syndrome (CIDS), a peripheral immunosuppressive state associated with increased infection risk. The endocannabinoid system, particularly cannabinoid receptor type 2 (CB2), represents a promising immunomodulatory target because of its anti-inflammatory actions and limited psychoactive liability. In this study, we investigated whether CB2 receptor activation confers neuroprotection and preserves systemic immune responsiveness in a murine photothrombotic stroke (PTS) model. Male C57BL/6 mice underwent PTS or sham surgery and were treated before stroke induction with the non-selective CB1/CB2 agonist WIN-55212, receptor antagonists, the selective CB2 agonist HU-308, or vehicle. Neurological deficits, infarct volume, cerebral inflammatory gene expression, and intestinal leukocyte-endothelial interactions following lipopolysaccharide (LPS) challenge were assessed using Neuroscore, TTC staining, RT-qPCR, and intravital microscopy. SIM-A9 microglia were used to evaluate the effects of HU-308 on viability and cytokine release under inflammatory conditions. PTS induced a CIDS-like phenotype characterized by reduced baseline leukocyte rolling and a markedly blunted leukocyte adhesion response following LPS challenge. Non-selective cannabinoid receptor activation improved neurological scores and reduced infarct size, while CB2 blockade abolished this protection. Selective CB2 activation with HU-308 reduced infarct volume, improved neurological outcome, and suppressed stroke-associated TNF and IL-6 expression in the ischemic hemisphere. In vitro, HU-308 reduced TNF release from LPS-stimulated microglia, while IL-4 enhanced microglial viability and IL-10 production. Importantly, HU-308 preserved leukocyte adhesion after LPS challenge following stroke, suggesting maintained peripheral immune responsiveness. These findings identify CB2 receptor activation as a promising neuroimmune strategy that limits acute stroke injury while attenuating the development of CIDS.

C.title: Inhibition of Endothelial Phosphodiesterase 2A Attenuates Post-infarct Inflammation.
C.abstract: After acute myocardial infarction (AMI), endothelial barrier dysfunction facilitates cardiac and sometimes remote pulmonary immune cell infiltration. Unraveling molecular pathways can provide targets for anti-inflammatory therapies. It is known that during bacterial pneumonia, tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α)-driven endothelial up-regulation of the dual phosphodiesterase (PDE) 2A, reducing cyclic nucleotide levels, fosters lung hyperpermeability. We studied whether PDE2A also participates in endothelial hyperpermeability after AMI. In mice, 2 days after experimental AMI, cardiac and pulmonary endothelial cell (EC) PDE2A expression was increased. This was concomitant with the induction of proinflammatory adhesion proteins and immune cell extravasation. In cultured microvascular myocardial and pulmonary ECs, TNF-α and interleukin-1β, cytokines released during cardiac ischemia, increased PDE2A expression through p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase activation. Conversely, the PDE2A inhibitor BAY 60-7550 enhanced endothelial 3',5'-cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) and 3',5'-cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) levels and attenuated thrombin-induced leakiness as well as TNF-α- or interleukin-1β-stimulated vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 and intercellular adhesion molecule 1 expression. To dissect the pathophysiological implications, we generated mice with EC-restricted PDE2A deletion (knockout). PDE2A ablation enhanced endothelial cGMP and cAMP levels and reduced cytokine-stimulated VCAM-1 expression. Accordingly, EC PDE2A knockout mice had diminished myocardial and pulmonary inflammation after AMI and reduced cardiac scarring and dysfunction. Our data indicate that endothelial induction of the cGMP and cAMP-degrading PDE2A participates in impaired cardiac and pulmonary microcirculatory barrier after AMI. Therefore, PDE2A might be a target for anti-inflammatory therapies.

C.title: [European guidelines for sclerotherapy in chronic venous disorders].
C.abstract:
AIM: Sclerotherapy is the targeted chemical ablation of varicose veins by intravenous injection of a liquid of foamed sclerosing drug. The treated veins may be intradermal, subcutaneous, and/or transfascial as well as superficial and deep in venous malformations. The aim of this guideline is to give evidence-based recommendations for liquid and foam sclerotherapy.
METHODS: This guideline was drafted on behalf of 23 European Phlebological Societies during Guideline Conference on 7-10 May 2012 in Mainz. The conference was organized by the German Society of Phlebology. These guidelines review the present state of knowledge as reflected in published medical literature. The regulatory situation of sclerosant drugs differs from country to country but this has not been considered in this document. The recommendations of this guiedeline are graded according to the American College of Chest Physicians Task Force recommendations on Grading Strenght of Recommendations and Quality of Evidence in Clinical Guidelines.
RESULTS: This guideline focuses on the two sclerosing drugs which are licensed in the majority of the European countries, polidokanol and sodium tetradecyl sulphate. Other sclerosants are dot discussed in detail. The guideline gives recommendations concerning indications, contraindications, side-effects, concentrations, volumes, technique and efficacy of liquid and foam sclerotherapy of varicose veins and venous malformations.

C.title: The Role of Extracorporeal Therapy in Light Chain Cast Nephropathy.
C.abstract:
BACKGROUND: A comparison of the efficacy of different extracorporeal platforms in reducing free light chain levels in the setting of light chain cast nephropathy has not been discussed in detail.
SUMMARY: Recent advances in treating multiple myeloma have increased overall survival and brought a cure closer to reality. Kidney failure remains one of the most significant factors impacting survival, and the recovery of kidney function is crucial in this aspect. Light chain cast nephropathy is the most common subtype of kidney injury caused by toxic monoclonal proteins in myeloma patients and is closely related to the concentration of the involved serum-free light chain (sFLC). A fast decline in sFLC is associated with improved kidney recovery rates. Negative results in randomized controlled trials of extracorporeal therapies have not yet distracted clinicians from applying these options in light chain cast nephropathy due to the demonstrated efficiency of these modalities in sFLC removal compared to conventional dialytic therapies. This review summarizes the efficiency of sFLC reduction with available extracorporeal methods in patients with multiple myeloma and severe kidney failure when combined with anti-myeloma therapy.
KEY MESSAGES: Since achieving a hematologic response is crucial in light chain cast nephropathy, it appears tough to demonstrate the possible benefit of extracorporeal FLC removal in cast nephropathy in this setting. High-cutoff hemodialysis reduces serum FLC by about 90% after several sessions when combined with anti-myeloma therapy, albeit with albumin loss. Other options, such as medium cutoff hemodialysis and adsorptive methods, may provide a less efficient removal with lower loss of plasma proteins. The contribution of extracorporeal therapy to renal recovery is still unclear.

C.title: Biomembrane-Camouflaged Stents: Promising Strategies for Advanced Coronary Interventions.
C.abstract: Coronary stent implantation remains a cornerstone therapy for coronary artery disease, yet current stent technologies continue to face limitations including acute and late thrombosis, delayed re-endothelialization, chronic inflammation, and in-stent restenosis. These complications largely arise from the nonphysiological interface between the implanted device and the injured vascular microenvironment. Biomembrane-camouflaged stents have recently emerged as a promising strategy to engineer biologically instructive blood-contacting surfaces by integrating natural or artificial membrane systems onto stent platforms. In this review, we summarize recent advances in three major biomembrane-based strategies for coronary stent functionalization: cell membrane-camouflaged stents, liposome-camouflaged stents, and exosome-camouflaged stents. Biomimetic cell membrane coatings retain native bioactive signals that collectively facilitate immune evasion, thromboresistance, and vascular healing. Liposome-based coatings are tunable artificial biomembrane reservoirs for the localized delivery of anticoagulants, anti-inflammatories, nitric oxide releasers, antiproliferatives, and gene therapies. Exosome-functionalized stents further enable bioactive intercellular communication by transferring endogenous regulatory cargos that modulate endothelial regeneration, macrophage polarization, smooth muscle cell phenotype, oxidative stress, and neointimal remodeling. We further discuss fabrication approaches, biological mechanisms, preclinical evidence, translational barriers, and future design principles for these platforms. Although challenges remain in coating durability, sterilization, long-term storage, manufacturing reproducibility, and clinical validation, biomembrane-camouflaged stents represent a compelling direction for next-generation coronary intervention by transforming conventional stents from passive mechanical scaffolds into active regulators of vascular repair.
