C.title: Intelligent immunotherapy: AI-driven optimization of CAR-T therapy in hematologic malignancies.
C.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed outcomes in selected hematologic malignancies, yet its delivery remains constrained by variable efficacy, acute and prolonged toxicities, and complex manufacturing logistics. Artificial intelligence (AI) is being applied across the CAR-T continuum at three distinct levels of evidentiary maturity. Externally validated parsimonious models built on routine clinical and laboratory data including CAR-HEMATOTOX, endothelial activation and stress index (EASIX) and m-EASIX, MyCARe, and gradient-boosting cytokine release syndrome predictors provide deployable risk stratification today. Methodologically sophisticated tools using deep-learning positron emission tomography (PET) segmentation, attention-based digital-pathology analysis, and multimodal fusion of imaging with laboratory and circulating tumor DNA features have demonstrated technical promise but generally lack the multi-center external validation required for clinical-grade deployment. Forward-looking applications, including digital-twin frameworks, large language models, and closed-loop adaptive therapy, remain at the prototype stage and have not yet been validated for CAR-T. This review synthesizes these three tiers, summarizes 18 published AI and statistical-modeling tools in a comparative performance table, and compares data characteristics and AI modeling paradigms across large B cell lymphoma, B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and multiple myeloma. We also identify the implementation realities-absent regulatory clearance, demographic and racial bias in training data, and post-deployment model drift-that condition the field's evolution. The contribution of AI to CAR-T therapy, as the evidence currently stands, is the calibrated quantification of established risk factors rather than the discovery of novel biology, but the methodological and data infrastructure foundations are now in place for the broader transformation that the next decade may enable.

C.title: Exploring the Pathogenesis and Treatment Strategies of Post-Herpetic Neuralgia Based on the "Gut-Immune-Neural Axis": A Narrative Review.
C.abstract: Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) is a prevalent and refractory neuropathic pain condition that arises after herpes zoster infection, characterized by complex pathophysiological mechanisms and limited efficacy of conventional treatments. Recent advances in the study of the gut-brain axis have expanded to encompass pain modulation, leading to the integrated concept of the "gut-immune-neural axis". This narrative review examines the proposed mechanisms by which gut microbiota may contribute to the onset and progression of PHN by modulating immune homeostasis, neuroinflammation, and neural plasticity. We explore the association between gut dysbiosis and PHN, highlighting the pivotal roles of microbial metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan derivatives in mediating these effects. Furthermore, we discuss emerging microbiota-targeted therapeutic strategies that target this axis to improve PHN management. Through a synthesis of current evidence, this narrative review aims to clarify the mechanistic hypotheses linking gut microbiota to PHN and to discuss potential or investigational therapeutic approaches grounded in gut microbiota modulation. It should be acknowledged that direct human evidence in PHN remains limited and largely observational, that much of the mechanistic support is extrapolated from preclinical models and other neuropathic pain conditions, and that the causal role of gut dysbiosis in PHN has not yet been established.

C.title: PET Imaging of Sphingolipid Signaling: Current Radiotracers, Translational Gaps, and Opportunities in Neurodegeneration and Oncology.
C.abstract: Sphingolipids regulate membrane organization, cell fate, and immune signaling in both health and disease. Dysregulation of the ceramide, sphingomyelin, and sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) pathways contribute to neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration, vascular injury, and cancer, motivating the development of in vivo imaging approaches to quantify sphingolipid signaling. Cellular homeostasis depends on a tightly regulated balance between pro-apoptotic ceramide and pro-survival S1P. Disruption of this balance, particularly through increased sphingosine kinase 1 (SPHK1/SK1) expression has been linked to aggressive tumor phenotypes and poor clinical outcomes. Recent advances in positron emission tomography (PET) have enabled imaging of select sphingolipid targets, including ceramide transport protein (CERT) and S1P receptor 1 (S1PR1), with one tracer progressing to first-in-human studies. While sphingolipid PET imaging has been applied in Alzheimer's disease (AD) research, translation to oncology remains limited despite the key role of sphingolipid metabolism in cancer biology and therapy. This review summarizes reported sphingolipid-targeted PET tracers, highlighting their biological rationale, radiochemical development, and preclinical and clinical applications, and emphasizes opportunities to advance sphingolipid PET imaging towards cancer imaging.

C.title: Harnessing cGAS-STING in neurodegeneration: From mitochondrial DNA leakage and microglial reactivity to species-specific translational barriers.
C.abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway, a cornerstone of innate immunity, has emerged as a critical driver of sterile neuroinflammation in the aging brain. Age-related decline in mitochondrial quality control, coupled with nuclear and lysosomal erosion, fosters the aberrant accumulation of cytosolic self-DNA, establishing a permissive environment for chronic cGAS-STING activation. This review synthesizes recent breakthroughs elucidating how major neurodegenerative diseases-Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Huntington's disease-converge on this pathway through distinct, disease-specific triggers, ranging from PINK1/Parkin deficiency-driven mitochondrial DNA leakage to TDP-43 proteinopathy-associated retrotransposon de-repression. Critically, we evaluate the translational landscape, highlighting the profound challenge posed by species-specific pharmacology, as exemplified by the failure of the covalent inhibitor H-151 to engage human STING. We argue that the future of therapeutic intervention lies not in wholesale pathway ablation, but in nuanced, context-dependent fine-tuning that disentangles its detrimental chronic effects from its indispensable homeostatic functions. This review positions the cGAS-STING axis as a promising yet delicate frontier for combating age-related neurodegeneration.

C.title: A cross-species AAV platform for precise microglial interrogation.
C.abstract: Targeting microglia with adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) remains challenging because of inefficient transduction, off-target expression, and inconsistent payload performance. Here, we develop an integrated, Cre-independent AAV platform that combines a compact 446-bp microglia-specific regulatory element (MSRE), a high-yield AAV2/9.m capsid, microRNA-mediated neuronal de-targeting, and a microglia-tailored codon-optimization strategy. Following direct intracranial delivery, the optimized vector achieves robust, long-lasting transgene expression with greater than 90% microglial specificity across multiple mouse brain regions, including in an Alzheimer's disease model. With doxorubicin-assisted delivery, the platform also enables efficient and selective microglial targeting in rats, rhesus macaques, and human ex vivo brain slices. Codon optimization supports the expression of otherwise challenging functional payloads, enabling calcium imaging, chemogenetic manipulation, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing. This cross-species toolkit provides a versatile resource for investigating microglial biology and developing microglia-directed therapeutic strategies.

C.title: Locoregionally delivered PD-1 blockade augments B7-H3 targeting CAR T cell efficacy in models of glioblastoma.
C.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a lethal brain tumor with a 95% five-year mortality rate, and remains a major unmet clinical need. An innovative approach to target GBM is administration of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells. In this study we identified B7-H3 as a favorable target antigen for CAR T cell therapy of GBM and developed a B7-H3 targeting CAR T cell. This CAR demonstrates robust, antigen-specific cytolysis and cytokine production, low tonic signaling, and preservation of a stem/naïve cell phenotype. Using orthotopic xenograft models of GBM we show that a single intravenous administration of this B7-H3 targeted CAR confers tumor control, and long-term survival. We identified upregulation of T cell inhibitory ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2 as a mechanism of resistance, and modified our B7-H3 targeting CAR vector to include a secreted a PD-1 blocking scFv. We further demonstrate that concomitant PD-1 blockade by the secreted PD-1 blocking scFv augments the antitumor capabilities of B7-H3-targeting CAR T cells through increased intratumoral infiltration by the CAR T cells and improved effector function. These data demonstrate B7-H3 targeting CAR T cells with concomitant PD-1 blockade is a safe and efficient method for improving the antitumor capacity of CAR T cells for GBM.

C.title: Inhibition of soluble epoxide hydrolase rescues cognitive deficits by preserving neurovascular integrity and attenuating glial and neuropathology in diabetic-related dementia.
C.abstract: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a major risk factor contributing to the development of Alzheimer's disease-related dementias (ADRD). While one of the early symptoms of both Alzheimer's disease (AD) and DM-related ADRD is a reduction in cerebral blood flow, the underlying biological mechanisms driving this decline remain to be fully elucidated. Genome-wide association studies have linked AD/ADRD to single-nucleotide polymorphisms in the gene encoding soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH), an enzyme we previously reported to be upregulated in the brains of an AD rat model. Our previous studies also demonstrated that chronic sEH inhibition with 1-trifluoromethoxyphenyl-3-(1-propionylpiperidin-4-yl) urea (TPPU) preserves hippocampal-dependent spatial learning and memory and improves cerebral hemodynamics in both AD and DM-ADRD models. In the present study, we found that chronic TPPU treatment (1 mg/kg/day) reduced sEH expression in the brain, improved cortical-based non-spatial recognition memory involving both cortical and hippocampal networks, and reduced anxiety in DM-ADRD rats. TPPU improved brain perfusion and normalized impaired whisker-evoked functional hyperemia, an effect associated with increased Kir2.1 expression and neurovascular coupling in cerebral capillaries. Furthermore, TPPU increased tight junction protein expression (ZO-1 and OCLN), mitigated capillary rarefaction, and suppressed astrocyte and microglial activation in DM-ADRD rats. At the cellular level, TPPU attenuated hippocampal neurodegeneration, restored the expression of synaptic proteins (PSD95 and SY38), and reduced levels of proinflammatory chemokines, including MCP-1, RANTES, and MIP-1α, in the hippocampus of DM-ADRD rats. In conclusion, TPPU preserves cognitive function in DM-ADRD by mitigating cerebrovascular dysfunction, neuroinflammation and gliosis, thereby preserving synaptic integrity and neuronal survival, and represents a promising therapeutic strategy for DM-ADRD.

C.title: Feasibility, Safety, and Effectiveness of Bleomycin Electrosclerotherapy in Patients with "Giant Hepatic Hemangiomas".
C.abstract: This retrospective study evaluated the feasibility, safety, and effectiveness of bleomycin electrosclerotherapy (BEST) in nine patients with symptomatic, size-progressive "giant hepatic hemangiomas" unsuitable for surgery. BEST was performed under general anesthesia using six CT-guided needle electrodes. Bleomycin was administered intravenously in three patients and intralesionally in six (3,000-16,430 IU). Follow-up MRI was recommended three months after treatment. Median volume reduction at first follow-up was 18.3% (IQR, 2.7%-36.2%; P = .020) at a median of 77 days (IQR, 44-117 days). Extended follow-up in eight patients demonstrated a median volume reduction of 47.0% (IQR, 17.5%-73.2%; P = .016) at 299 days (IQR, 256-739 days). Six of nine patients reported symptom improvement during follow-up. No major complications occurred; adverse events included three asymptomatic perihepatic hematomas and one intercostal neuralgia requiring prolonged analgesic treatment. BEST was feasible and associated with lesion volume reduction and symptom improvement in this cohort. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 4, Case Series.

C.title: Chronic spinal cord injury in a patient with Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome: Long-term rehabilitation challenges.
C.abstract:
CONTEXT: Spinal involvement in Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome (KTS) is uncommon, and long-term outcomes after extensive spinal surgery remain poorly characterized.
FINDINGS: A 64-year-old man with KTS developed progressive myelopathy and chronic incomplete thoracic spinal cord injury from an intraspinal vascular lesion causing cord compression. He underwent embolization, decompression, lesion resection, corrective osteotomies, and long-segment fusion. Over subsequent years, neurological and functional decline progressed with bilateral rod fractures, pseudoarthrosis, and sagittal imbalance. Rehabilitation produced modest functional gains without recovery of ambulation.
CONCLUSION: Long-term decline after spinal surgery in KTS may be multifactorial, supporting sustained multidisciplinary follow-up and rehabilitation.

C.title: [Protective effect of bloodletting at twelve Well-points of hand on neurological function by regulating cortical microglia/macrophage polarization through the IL-10/STAT1 pathway in mice with traumatic brain injury].
C.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To observe whether pricking blood therapy at the twelve Well points of the hand (Well-point bloodletting) can regulate the cortical phenotypic polarization of microglia and macrophages via the interleukin-10 (IL-10)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 1(STAT1) pathway, suppress excessive neuroinflammation and neuronal apoptosis, and thereby alleviate neurological deficits induced by traumatic brain injury (TBI) in mice.
METHODS: Male C57BL/6 mice were used in the present study which is composed of 3 experiments. The TBI model was established by using an electronically controlled cortical impact device to perform cortical impact. Experiment 1:Twelve mice randomly selected were used as the sham-operation group. Twenty-four TBI mice were randomly and equally divided into a model and a Well-point bloodletting group. Mice in the Well-point bloodletting group received interventions at 6 h, 24 h and 48 h after TBI respectively. The modified neurological severity score (mNSS) and open field test were used to assess the mouse's neurological deficits and locomotor function. Immunofluorescence staining was used to detect the proportions of apoptotic neurons (NeuN+TUNEL+) and microglia (IBA1+) in the injured cerebral cortex tissues. Liquid chip assay was performed to measure the levels of inflammatory factors in the injured cortical tissues, and Western blot was used to detect the expression of cortical STAT1 protein. Experiment 2:The STAT1 agonist 2-NP was applied to activate STAT1 to verify whether STAT1 mediates the anti-inflammatory effect of Well-point bloodletting. Thirty-six TBI mice were randomly and equally divided into model, Well-point bloodletting and Well-point bloodletting+2-NP groups. Mice in the Well-point bloodletting+2-NP group received intraperitoneal injection of 2-NP 1 h before modeling and each bloodletting intervention. The mNSS was used to assess the neurological function, and flow cytometry was utilized to quantify the proportions of M1 microglia and macrophages in the injured cerebral cortex. Experiment 3:this part of the study is conducted to clarify the pivotal role of IL-10 in the anti-inflammatory effect of Well-point bloodletting. The successfully modeled TBI mice were randomly allocated to the model, Well-point bloodletting and Well-point bloodletting+IL-10 antagonist groups, with 10 mice in each group. Mice in the IL-10 antagonist group received injection of IL-10 neutralizing antibody into the lateral ventricle on the contralateral side of the injured cortex 1 h after each bloodletting intervention to block the endogenous IL-10. The neurological deficits were evaluated using mNSS. Western blot was used to detect STAT1 phosphorylation in the brain tissues, and the flow cytometry was applied to measure the proportions of M1 microglia and macrophages in the injured cerebral cortex tissues.
RESULTS: Well-point bloodletting significantly reduced the mNSS scores at 6 h and 48 h (P<0.01, P<0.05) after TBI, down-regulated the proportions of apoptotic neurons and microglia (P<0.05, P<0.01), STAT1 phosphorylation (P<0.05) and IL-2 content (P<0.05), and increased the total travel distance 48 h after TBI (P<0.01) and IL-10 content (P<0.01). Well-point bloodletting+2-NP administration eliminated the effects of bloodletting in down-regulating the mNSS score after TBI (P<0.01) and the proportion of M1 microglia (P<0.01). Well-point bloodletting+IL-10 antagonist administration abolished the effects of Well-point bloodletting in lowering the mNSS score at 6, 24 and 48 h after TBI (P<0.05, P<0.01), suppressing STAT1 phosphorylation (P<0.05) and in reducing the proportions of M1 microglia and M1 macrophages in the injured cerebral cortex (P<0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: Well-point bloodletting can improve the neurological deficits and motor function in TBI mice, which may be related to its functions in inhibiting M1 polarization of microglia and macrophages through the IL-10/STAT1 pathway, and mitigating cortical neuroinflammation and neuronal apoptosis.

C.title: [Mechanism of electroacupuncture combined with antibiotics targeting dorsal motor nucleus of vagus nerve to activate vagus-adrenal axis, alleviate inflammatory response and reduce mortality in septic mice].
C.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To explore the mechanism by which electroacupuncture (EA) combined with antibiotics regulates the vagus-adrenal axis via the dorsal motor nucleus of vagus (DMV), promotes catecholamine secretion, attenuates inflammatory storm, and improves survival rate in septic mice.
METHODS: Experiment 1:fifty C57BL/6 mice were randomly divided into sham operation group, model group, antibiotic group, EA group, and EA + antibiotic group, with 10 mice in each group. Cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) was performed to establish the sepsis model. Mice in the EA group received 15 min EA (10 Hz, 0.5 mA) at bilateral "Zusanli" (ST36), once daily for 3 consecutive days. Mice in the antibiotic group were intraperitoneally injected with imipenem-cilastatin sodium (30 mg/kg) every 12 h for 3 consecutive days. Mice in the EA+antibiotic group received EA and antibiotic treatment the same as the above. The 3-day survival rate and body weight changes of mice in each group were recorded. ELISA was adopted to detect serum levels of interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α). HE staining was used to observe pathological changes and the number of inflammatory cells in cecal tissues. Whole-brain optical clearing was performed to detect the expression of proto-oncogene c-Fos protein (c-Fos) in the DMV region. Experiment 2:fifty Chat-Cre mice were randomly assigned to sham operation + empty virus group, model + empty virus group, EA-antibiotic combination + empty virus group, EA-antibiotic combination + inhibitory virus group, and antibiotic + activating virus group, with 10 mice per group. Corresponding viruses were injected into the DMV 3 weeks before model establishment. CLP operation was conducted 3 weeks after virus injection, followed by daily intraperitoneal injection of clozapine N-oxide (CNO, 3 mg/kg), combined with antibiotics or EA treatment (the same interventions and parameters as Experiment 1). Serum IL-6 and TNF-α levels were measured by ELISA;cecal inflammatory infiltration was evaluated via HE staining. Ultra-high performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) was applied to detect serum catecholamines including dopamine (DA), epinephrine (E), norepinephrine (NE), as well as their metabolites 3-methoxytyramine (3-MT), normetanephrine (NMN), and metanephrine (MN) levels. Immunofluorescence staining was used to quantify the counts of forkhead box protein P3 positive / cluster of differentiation 4 positive (FOXP3+/CD4+) cells in cecal tissues.
RESULTS: Experiment 1:compared with the sham operation group, the model group exhibited markedly decreased 3-day survival rate and body weight (P<0.000 1), elevated serum IL-6 and TNF-α levels (P<0.000 1), and increased inflammatory cell infiltration in cecum (P<0.000 1). Compared with the model group, the EA + antibiotic group showed improved survival rate (P<0.05), alleviated body weight loss (P<0.000 1), decreased serum IL-6 and TNF-α levels (P<0.000 1), reduced inflammatory cell infiltration (P<0.000 1), and elevated c-Fos positive cell density in DMV (P<0.000 1). Moreover, all above indicators were superior to those in the single EA or single antibiotic group to varying degrees. Experiment 2:in comparison with the sham operation + empty virus group, the model + empty virus group had higher serum inflammatory factor levels and more cecal inflammatory infiltrates (P<0.0001), and lower levels of catecholamines and their metabolites, as well as fewer FOXP3+/CD4+ cells in cecal tissues (P<0.000 1). Compared with the model + empty virus group, the EA-antibiotic combination + empty virus group, EA-antibiotic combination + inhibitory virus group, and antibiotic + activating virus group displayed reduced serum inflammatory factors and relieved cecal inflammatory infiltration (P<0.000 1, P<0.01, P<0.05), accompanied by increased levels of catecholamines and metabolites, and more FOXP3+/CD4+ cells in cecum (P<0.01, P<0.05, P<0.001, P<0.000 1). Relative to the EA-antibiotic combination + empty virus group, all the above indicators were reversed in the EA-antibiotic combination + inhibitory virus group (P<0.01, P<0.001, P<0.05, except for 3-MT).
CONCLUSIONS: EA at ST36 combined with antibiotics exerts optimal therapeutic effects on CLP-induced septic mice. The underlying mechanism may involve activating cholinergic neurons in DMV, regulating the vagus-adrenal axis to facilitate catecholamine secretion, suppressing excessive inflammatory response, and consequently elevating survival rate.

C.title: [Comparative study on intervention effects of electroacupuncture at single point "Zusanli" (ST36), "Sanyinjiao" (SP6) and combined points on irritable bowel syndrome mice].
C.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To compare the differences in interventional effects among three stimulation modalities:electroacupuncture (EA) at single acupoint "Zusanli" (ST36), single acupoint "Sanyinjiao" (SP6), and their combination (ST36 + SP6), on behavioral and histological outcomes in a mouse model of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), and to examine the differential neuronal responses in the peripheral and central nervous systems under these modalities, so as to provide experimental evidence for exploring the neural mechanisms underlying acupoint combination stimulation in IBS treatment.
METHODS: An IBS model was established in male C57BL/6J mice by intrarectal instillation of zymosan. The mice were randomly divided into blank control group, model group, ST36 group, SP6 group, and acupoint combination group (n=20 per group except n=18 for the model group). After 7 consecutive days of EA stimulation (2 Hz/100 Hz, 1 mA, 15 min per session, once daily), abdominal mechanical hyperalgesia (referred pain) was assessed using von Frey filaments, motor function by rotarod test, and 3D spontaneous fine behavioral characteristics by an AI-based unsupervised 3D behavioral analysis system. Colon tissue structure and inflammatory levels were observed by HE staining, and colonic inflammatory cytokine expressions were detected by Western blot, to evaluate the symptom-relieving effects of single versus combined acupoint stimulation. For neural tracing, retrograde viral tracers were injected into ST36 and SP6 to label dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons innervating these acupoints in C57BL/6J mice. In vivo two-photon calcium imaging was performed to record DRG neuronal responses to different EA modalities (1 mA, 1 min) in Thy1-GCaMP6s mice, and activity-dependent neuronal labeling was applied using transgenic TRAP2;Ai14 mice to identify central neurons activated by EA (2 Hz/100 Hz, 1 mA, 15 min per session), aiming to reveal peripheral-central neuronal response differences between single and combined acupoint stimulation.
RESULTS: Compared with the blank control group, the model group showed increased abdominal mechanical withdrawal frequency and area under the curve (P<0.001, P<0.05), decreased motor function (latency to fall and rotarod speed at fall, P<0.01), aggravated colonic tissue damage and inflammatory responses (P<0.001), elevated expressions of interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α, P<0.001), and altered spontaneous behavioral patterns (P<0.001, P<0.01, P<0.05). All three EA modalities significantly alleviated abdominal mechanical hyperalgesia in IBS mice (P<0.001, P<0.05, P<0.01), with the combined stimulation showing a larger effective interventional window than either single acupoint. Compared with single-acupoint stimulation, combined stimulation also more effectively restored colonic tissue damage, reduced TNF-α expression (P<0.05), and shortened the duration of spontaneous arching episodes and altered the transition patterns among different spontaneous behavioral actions (P<0.01, P<0.05). DRG neurons exhibited highly heterogeneous responses to the three stimulation modalities, which could be classified into 3 major categories and 7 subcategories based on their firing characteristics. Furthermore, combined stimulation activated a greater number of DRG neurons than single acupoint stimulation (P<0.05), and the neuronal calcium signal intensity was also higher (P<0.05). Finally, significant differences were observed in the number of responsive neurons across different brain regions under the three modalities. The activated neuronal populations evoked by ST36, SP6, and combined stimulation showed maximal overlap in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN), whereas the overlap was minimal in the insular cortex (IC), suggesting that IC neuronal activation requires the synergistic effect of combined acupoint stimulation.
CONCLUSIONS: Combined stimulation at ST36 and SP6 produces superior therapeutic effects over single acupoint stimulation in ameliorating abdominal mechanical hyperalgesia, colonic structural damage, inflammatory status, and spontaneous behavioral changes induced by visceral pain in IBS model mice, and this advantage may arise from the synergistic integration of peripheral and central neuronal responses to different EA signals.

C.title: β-Asarone Alleviates Post-stroke Neuroinflammation and Improves Mitochondrial Quality Via the BNIP3/BNIP3L-dependent Mitophagy Pathway.
C.abstract: Ischemic stroke (IS) is a leading cause of death and disability worldwide, with mitophagy playing a central role in post-stroke neurological dysfunction. β-Asarone, a major bioactive component derived from the traditional herb Acorus tatarinowii, possesses antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective properties. However, whether β-asarone ameliorates IS by regulating mitophagy and its underlying mechanisms remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate whether β-asarone exerts neuroprotective effects against IS by modulating BNIP3/BNIP3L-mediated mitophagy. A middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) rat model and an oxygen-glucose deprivation/reperfusion (OGD/R) cell model were established. Neuroprotective effects were evaluated using neurological behavioral scores, 2,3,5-triphenyltetrazolium chloride (TTC) staining, hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) staining, and Nissl staining. Mitochondrial function was assessed by measuring reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP). Mitophagy was observed via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and fluorescence microscopy. Western blot (WB) analysis was performed to detect BNIP3/BNIP3L pathway proteins. Results showed that β-asarone enhanced mitophagy, improved mitochondrial function, and alleviated post-stroke neuroinflammation. Conversely, the autophagy inhibitor 3-methyladenine (3-MA) impaired mitophagic function, exacerbating ischemia-induced brain injury and inflammation, while β-asarone treatment reversed these detrimental effects. In summary, β-asarone mitigates neuroinflammation and neuronal injury after IS, at least partly through promoting BNIP3/BNIP3L-mediated mitophagy, highlighting this pathway as a promising therapeutic target for IS.

C.title: GNAI2 activating variants and MAGIS syndrome: long-term endocrine and growth outcome.
C.abstract:
CONTEXT: Germline activating variants in the GNAI2 gene have recently been associated with MAGIS syndrome, characterized by midline malformations of the brain, anterior pituitary gland dysfunction, growth retardation, immunodysregulation, and skeletal defects. However, the full phenotypic spectrum, particularly regarding endocrine dysfunction, remains incompletely defined.
CASE DESCRIPTION: We report on a 9.5-year-old male presenting with MAGIS syndrome due to a de novo GNAI2 (NM_002070.4):c.544A>C, p.(Thr182Pro) variant. He initially presented at 17 months with short stature and hypopituitarism. Pituitary MRI confirmed anterior pituitary hypoplasia with thin stalk and normal posterior pituitary. Long-term follow-up revealed suboptimal response to recombinant growth hormone therapy with persistent low IGF-1, profound prolactin deficiency, and evolving gonadotropin deficiency. He also had delayed developmental milestones, recurrent infections, chronic diarrhea, subclinical hypothyroidism, and skeletal abnormalities. Immunological evaluation showed low T-cell counts, inadequate antibody responses and no overt autoimmune features apart from infantile atopic dermatitis.
CONCLUSIONS: This report details the longitudinal clinical, endocrine, and growth data in a patient with MAGIS syndrome harboring a GNAI2 p.Thr182Pro variant. It highlights the suboptimal growth response to GH with fluctuating height velocity and the development of additional endocrine abnormalities such as prolactin, thyroid dysfunction and suspected gonadotropin deficiency. Detailed phenotypic characterization in such cases is crucial for understanding this complex genetic disorder.

C.title: Apelin-13 exerts neuroprotection through activation of APJ/mTORC2 axis in microglia after Intracerebral Hemorrhage in mice.
C.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Apelin-13, a bioactive peptide that acts via the APJ receptor, exhibits potent anti-oxidant, anti-apoptotic, and anti-inflammatory properties. However, its role in intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) remains poorly understood. In this study, we aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential of Apelin-13 and the underlying mechanisms in a mouse model of ICH.
METHODS: A mouse model of intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) was established and randomly allocated to receive either recombinant Apelin-13 (rApelin-13) or phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). To investigate the role of the APJ/mammalian target of rapamycin complex 2 (mTORC2) axis in Apelin-13-mediated neuroprotection, the APJ antagonist ML221 and the mTORC2 inhibitor JR-AB2-011 were administered. To further elucidate the underlying mechanism, microglia-specific knockdown of Rictor was achieved via intracerebroventricular injection of an adeno-associated virus (AAV) carrying CD68-promoter-driven shRictor. Assessments included brain water content, short-term neurobehavioral tests, Western blot analysis, quantitative RT-PCR, and histological staining.
RESULTS: Following ICH induction, the expression of Apelin-13 was upregulated and primarily secreted from neurons. Exogenous administration of rApelin-13 significantly attenuated neuronal apoptosis and improved short-term neurological function in mice after ICH in a dose-dependent manner. Furthermore, rApelin-13 enhanced M2-like polarization of microglia in the post-ICH brain. Notably, the neuroprotective effects of rApelin-13 were abolished by inhibition of mTORC2.

C.title: PHLDA3 deficiency attenuates neonatal sepsis-associated acute lung injury and is associated with reduced endoplasmic reticulum stress and NF-κB activation.
C.abstract: Neonatal sepsis often causes acute lung injury (ALI), but the underlying molecular mechanisms of ALI have not been elucidated. Pleckstrin homology-like domain family A member 3 (PHLDA3) is a stress-responsive protein involved in inflammatory signaling, yet its role in neonatal sepsis-associated ALI has not been explored. Here, we established a neonatal polymicrobial sepsis model via intraperitoneal injection of cecal slurry (CS) and investigated the role of PHLDA3 in ALI using CRISPR/Cas9-generated constitutive PHLDA3 knockout (PHLDA3 KO) mice. CS induced time-dependent upregulation of PHLDA3 in neonatal lung tissues. CS triggered significant increases in the levels of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α in lung tissues, impairing vascular integrity and causing severe alveolar damage. These harmful effects were alleviated by PHLDA3 KO. Transcriptomic analysis revealed enrichment of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) protein processing pathways. CS activated ER stress and unfolded protein response via PERK/eIF2α/ATF4 and ATF6 axes, which were attenuated by PHLDA3 deletion. Pharmacological induction of ER stress by thapsigargin (TG) reversed the protective effects of PHLDA3 KO, whereas ER stress inhibitor 4-phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA) mitigated inflammation and lung injury. In macrophage models, PHLDA3 knockdown was associated with reduced LPS-induced ER-stress-related signaling, NF-κB activation, and inflammatory responses, whereas TG attenuated these effects. Collectively, these findings indicate that constitutive PHLDA3 deficiency is associated with attenuated neonatal sepsis-associated lung injury, reduced ER-stress-related signaling, and decreased NF-κB activation, and support further investigation of PHLDA3 in neonatal sepsis-associated ALI.

C.title: BCG vaccination mitigates tau pathology and restores cognitive function in PS19 mice.
C.abstract: Retrospective studies in patients with nonmuscle invasive bladder cancer have reported a significant reduction in Alzheimer's disease incidence (12 to 78%) among Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) recipients versus controls. To investigate the underlying mechanisms, we evaluated BCG in the PS19 mouse model of tauopathy. We found that BCG administration reduced hippocampal phospho-tau and microgliosis while preserving neuronal markers. In vivo volumetric T2-magnetic resonance Imaging (MRI) demonstrated attenuation of brain atrophy accompanied by increased glutamate-weighted chemical exchange saturation transfer-MRI signals. Functionally, BCG-treated mice showed improved performance in the novel object recognition test, as well as improved body-weight maintenance and survival. Transcriptomic profiling of the hippocampus revealed near complete normalization of the PS19 disease-associated gene expression signature toward that of healthy controls. Flow cytometric profiling of brain myeloid populations demonstrated a reduction in activated resident microglia, but total microglia cells remain elevated. Moreover, an increase of trained immunity marker CD80 on the recruited peripheral myeloid cells ensues following BCG treatment. Consistent with this shift in myeloid state, primary brain myeloid cells from BCG-treated mice also exhibited enhanced phagocytosis of fluorescein isothiocyanate-labeled tau fibrils and increased lactate production. Together, these findings indicate that BCG induces systemic and central nervous system myeloid cell reprogramming that limits neuroinflammation, enhances tau clearance, and rescues cognitive and neurodegenerative phenotypes in a tauopathy model. BCG is a safe, readily available therapy that merits consideration as a preventive agent against dementia.

C.title: Serine protease inhibitor A3 is a soluble SIRPα ligand that suppresses inflammation and antitumor immunity.
C.abstract: SIRPα is an inhibitory receptor with the canonical ligand CD47. Here, we show that human serine protease inhibitor A3 (SERPINA3) and its mouse ortholog SERPINA3k function as soluble binders and activators of SIRPα, suppressing SIRPα+ macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells and natural killer cells. SERPINA3(k) treatment alleviates lipopolysaccharide-induced pneumonia and ameliorates experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis and rheumatoid arthritis. Although wild-type SERPINA3 provokes inflammation in cardiomyocytes and brain vascular endothelial cells, the SERPINA3D2 mutant, identified through functional domain mapping for SIRPα interaction, abolishes these adverse effects while retaining full inhibitory capacity. Notably, cancer cells secrete large amounts of SERPINA3(k), exceeding CD47 levels. Anti-SERPINA3(k) antibodies, used alone or in combination with blockade of programmed cell death 1 receptor/programmed cell death ligand 1, inhibit tumor growth in multiple preclinical models. This work identifies a potent soluble SIRPα ligand, offering effective therapeutic strategies for inflammatory/autoimmune diseases and a promising target for cancer immunotherapy.
